## DAILY SECURITY BRIEF

### 1. Russia and Ukraine intensify long-range attacks
Ukraine launched one of its largest drone barrages of the war, with Russia claiming 822 drones intercepted nationwide and about 600 directed toward Moscow. At least six people were reported killed in Russia. Russian missile and drone strikes killed at least five people in Ukraine, damaged the ArcelorMittal plant in Kryvyi Rih and destroyed part of a major Kyiv book market.

**Why it matters:** Both sides are expanding attacks far behind the front, increasing pressure on air defenses, industrial capacity and civilian populations. The reported scale of the interceptions has not been independently verified.

### 2. NATO fighter downs drone over Romania
A Spanish F-18 on NATO air-policing duty shot down a drone after it entered Romanian airspace from the direction of Moldova. NATO said the aircraft appeared to be Russian, although the incident remains under investigation. It followed recent drone interceptions over Latvia.

**Why it matters:** Repeated incursions increase the risk that the Russia-Ukraine conflict spills into NATO territory and prompt more forceful alliance responses.

### 3. Ukraine targets Russian missile and logistics infrastructure
Ukraine said it struck a Bastion coastal missile system in occupied Crimea, a platform Russia uses to launch Oniks and Zircon missiles. Kyiv also reported attacks on a Russian solid-rocket-fuel plant, a railway bridge and ammunition and logistics facilities. Damage assessments remain incomplete.

**Why it matters:** Targeting launchers, production sites and supply routes is intended to reduce Russian strike capacity at its source, particularly as Ukraine faces shortages of ballistic-missile interceptors.

### 4. North Korean support for Russia may expand
Ukrainian and international intelligence agencies reportedly suspect North Korea could send another 30,000–50,000 troops to Russia. Ukraine also says Pyongyang has supplied KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles and may deploy a missile unit to Russia’s Voronezh region. Analysts cited in the reporting said firm evidence of a large new troop deployment is not yet available.

**Why it matters:** Additional North Korean personnel could release Russian forces for frontline operations, while more ballistic missiles would compound Ukraine’s critical Patriot-interceptor shortage.

### 5. US-Iran impasse continues over the Strait of Hormuz
A deadline for Washington and Tehran to reach an understanding on reopening the Strait of Hormuz passed without an agreement. Iran says reopening depends on the United States meeting its conditions; Washington is demanding that Iran first end the blockade. Oman-mediated contacts continue amid escalating rhetoric.

**Why it matters:** Prolonged disruption of the strait threatens energy supplies, shipping and global economic stability, while the absence of an agreement leaves open the risk of renewed military escalation.

## WATCH

- **North Korean deployments:** Confirmation of additional troops or missile units entering Russia, and whether they operate beyond Russian territory.
- **Ukraine’s deep-strike campaign:** Verified damage to the Bastion system and Russian missile-production facilities, alongside Ukraine’s reported effort to field domestic ballistic missiles.
- **Middle East diplomacy and escalation:** Cairo talks involving Hamas and US envoy Jared Kushner, and whether renewed Israeli strikes in Lebanon undermine the June ceasefire.

regional_summaries.asia:
## 1. North Korea and Russia reaffirm expanding partnership

**What happened:** Kim Jong Un and Vladimir Putin exchanged messages pledging broader cooperation during commemorations of Korea’s liberation from Japanese rule. A Russian ship also made a goodwill visit to North Korea’s Wonsan port. The relationship has deepened through North Korean troop deployments and weapons support for Russia’s war in Ukraine.

**Why it matters:** The partnership gives Russia additional military resources while providing North Korea with a major strategic partner. Expanded cooperation could strengthen Pyongyang’s military capabilities and complicate efforts to isolate it over its nuclear and missile programs.

## 2. South Korea proposes talks on a permanent peace framework

**What happened:** South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for dialogue with North Korea, conflict-prevention safeguards and replacement of the Korean War armistice with a formal “peace regime.” He said negotiations could also address North Korea’s nuclear program. Pyongyang has rejected Lee’s overtures and continues to criticize US-South Korean exercises.

**Why it matters:** Seoul is signaling an effort to reduce tensions and reopen diplomacy, but North Korea’s rejection leaves little immediate prospect of progress. The peninsula remains technically at war and vulnerable to escalation through military exercises, missile launches or miscalculation.

## 3. Regional concern grows over missile launches and Chinese military pressure

**What happened:** Forty countries, including Ukraine, signed a declaration calling for at least 24 hours’ advance notice of intercontinental ballistic missile, submarine-launched missile and space-launch vehicle tests. The initiative followed reported Chinese and North Korean launches. Separately, Taiwan tracked 11 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels and two official ships near the island; seven aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line.

**Why it matters:** Advance-notification mechanisms could reduce risks to civilian aviation and shipping and limit unintended escalation. Continued Chinese operations around Taiwan, however, demonstrate sustained military pressure and increase the potential for incidents in the Taiwan Strait.

## WATCH

- Whether North Korea expands troop or weapons support for Russia, and whether Moscow provides significant military or technological assistance in return.
- The frequency and scale of Chinese operations around Taiwan, particularly median-line crossings and any movement beyond routine “gray-zone” pressure.
regional_summaries.europe_russia:
## 1. Russia and Ukraine Intensify Long-Range Strikes

Ukraine launched one of its largest reported drone attacks of the war, targeting Moscow, Rostov and other Russian regions. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed 822 drones were intercepted overnight, although the scale was not independently verified. Russian authorities reported at least six deaths, damage to homes and logistics facilities, and significant disruption at Moscow airports.

Russia simultaneously conducted missile and drone strikes across Ukraine, killing at least five people and damaging civilian and industrial sites. ArcelorMittal’s Kryvyi Rih steel plant partially suspended operations after core facilities were hit. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided bombs and 62 missiles during the preceding week.

**Why it matters:** The attacks demonstrate the increasing scale and reach of both countries’ deep-strike capabilities. They are placing greater pressure on air defenses, industrial production, logistics networks and civilian populations far from the front.

## 2. NATO Jet Downs Drone Over Romania

A Spanish F-18 operating on NATO air-policing duties shot down a drone after it entered Romanian airspace near the borders with Ukraine and Moldova. Debris reportedly fell in an unpopulated area. Romanian authorities did not initially identify the drone’s origin, while a NATO spokesperson said it appeared to be Russian.

**Why it matters:** The interception highlights the growing risk that the Russia-Ukraine drone war will spill into NATO territory. Repeated incursions increase the possibility of escalation and are likely to prompt stronger surveillance and air-defense measures along NATO’s eastern flank.

## 3. Ukraine Targets Russian Bastion Missile System in Crimea

The Ukrainian Navy said it struck launch positions and a deployment site for a Russian Bastion coastal missile system near Sevastopol in occupied Crimea. Ukraine reported significant equipment and personnel losses, but the extent of the damage remains under assessment. Russia uses Bastion systems to launch Oniks and Zircon missiles against Ukrainian targets.

**Why it matters:** Damaging the relatively scarce launch system could reduce Russia’s capacity to conduct difficult-to-intercept missile attacks from Crimea. The operation also reinforces Ukraine’s campaign against Russian military infrastructure and logistics on the peninsula.

## WATCH

- **Long-range weapons development:** Ukraine says domestically produced ballistic missiles could become available within three to six months, while Poland is planning precision-strike capabilities beyond 1,000 kilometers.
- **Air-defense pressure:** Monitor Ukraine’s interceptor shortages and any additional NATO responses to drone incursions along the alliance’s eastern border.
regional_summaries.middle_east:
### 1. US–Iran talks lapse as Hormuz confrontation persists

The 60-day negotiating period established by the June interim agreement ended without a broader settlement or the full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran says reopening depends on Washington meeting conditions including sanctions relief and access to frozen assets; the US demands that Iran first end restrictions on shipping. Washington is preparing additional sanctions and maintains a naval blockade, while both sides continue issuing threats.

**Why it matters:** The strait previously carried about one-fifth of globally traded oil and natural gas. Continued disruption risks higher energy prices, wider economic damage and renewed US–Iran military exchanges. Additional US sanctions could also affect Chinese refiners and banks, potentially broadening the dispute.

### 2. Gaza diplomacy resumes but core terms remain contested

Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya and US envoy Jared Kushner were in Cairo for talks involving Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators. The proposed roadmap calls for Hamas’s disarmament, an Israeli withdrawal and administration of Gaza by Palestinian technocrats. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the latest proposal, insisting that Hamas disarm before Israel withdraws from territory it controls. Israeli airstrikes in Gaza have also resumed.

**Why it matters:** The negotiations represent a renewed attempt to turn the ceasefire into a durable political arrangement and begin reconstruction. However, disagreement over sequencing, Israeli military operations and Hamas’s disarmament remains a major obstacle and could lead to renewed large-scale fighting.

### 3. Fighting intensifies again in Yemen

Missile and drone attacks struck government-held Marib and the Red Sea port city of Mocha. Yemeni government and local media reports attributed the attacks to the Houthis, who had not commented. Reports said four people were killed and others wounded in Mocha, while strikes damaged residential areas in Marib. Government forces reported extensive retaliatory operations against Houthi positions.

**Why it matters:** The escalation threatens to end the relative lull that had largely held since 2022. Renewed fighting around Marib and Mocha could worsen Yemen’s humanitarian crisis and create additional security risks near Red Sea trade routes.

### WATCH

- **Lebanon:** Israel has threatened further escalation after heavy strikes reportedly killed at least 11 people, raising the risk that the ceasefire with Hezbollah will unravel.
- **Iraq:** Continued drone attacks on the Kurdistan Region highlight Baghdad’s difficulty controlling Iran-backed militias and protecting coalition-linked sites.
regional_summaries.america_other:
### 1. Air Force seeks DJI drones for nuclear-site defense training

The U.S. Air Force issued a solicitation for several Chinese-made DJI drones at F.E. Warren Air Force Base, which supports Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles. Security personnel would use them to test radar, jamming and other counter-drone systems against DJI’s actual signals and flight characteristics. Modified software is intended to prevent data transfers.

**Why it matters:** DJI dominates the commercial drone market, making its aircraft representative of likely threats to military installations. However, deploying Chinese-made systems at a nuclear missile base raises supply-chain and cybersecurity concerns despite planned safeguards.

### 2. Navy directed to examine return to steam catapults

President Donald Trump issued a national security memorandum directing the Navy to develop a plan to replace electromagnetic aircraft launch systems with conventional steam catapults on future carriers. The administration characterized steam systems as more proven, reliable and affordable.

**Why it matters:** Reversing the Ford-class launch-system design could require extensive engineering changes, add billions of dollars in costs and worsen shipbuilding delays. It could also affect carrier sortie generation, maintenance requirements and long-term fleet modernization.

### 3. Ford-class carrier island redesign under consideration

The Navy is reportedly assessing whether to move the Ford-class carrier’s command island forward, giving future ships an appearance closer to older carrier designs. The island was originally positioned farther aft to improve deck operations, aircraft movement and landing safety. A previous study reportedly found that relocation would be costly and disruptive.

**Why it matters:** A major structural redesign could delay future carriers and increase costs that are already estimated at roughly $22 billion per ship. Changing a configuration chosen for operational reasons may also affect flight-deck efficiency and safety.

### WATCH

- Whether Congress and the Navy approve, limit or reject proposed Ford-class design and catapult changes.
- Whether the Air Force expands the use of DJI drones for counter-drone training at other nuclear missile bases and what cybersecurity controls are imposed.

articles.title: Russia Unveils Jet-Powered BM-35 Drone With 217 Mph Speed
articles.body:
Russian propagandists have aired a segment showcasing the use of a jet-powered BM-35 attack drone, which they claim can reach speeds exceeding 350 km/h (217 mph) and cover distances up to 200 km (124 miles).
Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to President Volodymyr Zelensky, highlighted the report regarding the drone’s capabilities.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to the Russian operators featured in the segment, the BM-35 does not require complex preparation. They stated the drone can be launched within minutes from any terrain using a mobile platform.
The propagandists claimed that an operator can control the drone throughout its entire flight trajectory, essentially in a First-Person View (FPV) mode. They further asserted that Ukrainian electronic warfare (EW) systems do not affect the drone’s signal.
The BM-35 reportedly carries a 22-pounds warhead. The operators claimed the 124-mile range allows them to strike targets deep in the rear, while the speed of over 217 mph prevents Ukrainian interceptors from catching the apparatus.
According to the report, the components are prepared in advance at a warehouse, leaving only the assembly of the drone, installation of the warhead, and the launch to be completed at the firing position.
The operators stated that up to three drones can be launched simultaneously and that the warhead disperses up to a thousand fragmentation elements over a 650-feet (198-meter) radius upon detonation.
Drone Attacks Spark Large Fires at Wildberries Hubs Near Moscow
Foreign components in Russian weapons
The development follows recent reports from Ukraine’s military intelligence (HUR) regarding the integration of advanced foreign technology into new Russian weapons systems.
On Aug. 12, HUR reported that its specialists had identified an Nvidia Jetson Orin computer module inside Russia’s new S-71 Monochrome air-launched cruise missile.
The agency stated that the use of this module potentially indicates the integration of artificial intelligence technologies into the weapon.
The finding was published on the HUR’s War&Sanctions portal, which documents foreign electronic components found in Russian weapons. The intelligence agency noted that the latest research identified 35 foreign electronic components in the S-71 Monochrome.
Ukrainian specialists have also identified parts of a passive radar seeker that Russia has begun installing on Geran-2 drones, designed to detect and strike Ukrainian air-defense systems.
Additionally, researchers identified a Chinese Honpho TS130C-01 camera from a Geran-4 jet-powered drone and components of the active radar seeker used in Russia’s Kh-47M2 Kinzhal aeroballistic missile.
HUR stated that the continued discovery of foreign high-tech components demonstrates that Russia has been unable to fully replace them with domestic alternatives, underscoring the need for increased sanctions pressure.
The agency noted that limited production capacity prevents Russian forces from maintaining continuous, high-intensity drone launches, forcing them to build up reserves prior to major attacks.

articles.title: Strikes kill 12 in Russia and Ukraine
articles.body:
The warring countries have significantly stepped up long-range attacks deep behind each other's lines. (STRINGER / AFP)
Overnight strikes killed 12 people in Russia and Ukraine, authorities said on Aug. 16, as waves of drones and missiles pummeled civilian infrastructure on both sides.
With fighting at the front at a near standstill and talks frozen, the warring countries have significantly stepped up long-range attacks deep behind each other's lines, pushing the civilian death toll to its highest levels since the war's first months in 2022.
In Russia, swarms of Ukrainian drones killed five people in a residential area of the southern Rostov region, regional governor Yuri Slusar said. Two more people were killed in the Belgorod and Moscow regions.
Moscow regional governor Andrey Vorobyov described the assault as "one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory". Russia's defense ministry said it had intercepted 822 drones across the country overnight.
In Ukraine, a barrage of Russian drones and missiles killed two people and wounded 14 at ArcelorMittal's steel plant in Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown. The plant, one of Ukraine's biggest steel producers, said it partially halted operations after the strike damaged its core production facilities.
Strikes also hit other regions, killing two people in the southeastern Zaporizhzhia region and one in the border region of Sumy.
In Kiev, a popular outdoor book market at Pochaina, long the place to find rare and antiquarian volumes, was struck. Bookseller Dmytro Semenukha saw all four of his stalls burn to the ground.
"There used to be a store. And books, and flags of all the countries, all the countries. Tons of everything. And that's it," the 45-year-old told AFP.
In a social media post on the overnight raid, Zelensky said "wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure."
Over the past week, he said, Ukrainian cities had been pummeled by "more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles", as he renewed his appeal to allies for more air defense.
Russia has carried out near-daily missile and drone strikes across Ukraine since launching its full-scale invasion in early 2022. It has recently intensified attacks using hard-to-intercept ballistic missiles, exploiting Ukraine's air-defense shortages after the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran diverted supplies.
"When North Korean ballistic missiles destroy infrastructure and claim lives here in Europe, European interceptors cannot simply be allowed to sit in storage," Zelensky said. Kiev has recently renewed claims that Moscow is receiving more missiles and troops from its ally North Korea.
Countries bordering the conflict have meanwhile faced increasing spillover from the drone war. After the overnight raid, Romania's defense ministry said a Spanish F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that breached its airspace near the borders with Ukraine and Moldova.
NATO said on Aug. 14 that its fighter jets shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace — the second such incident there in a week, according to Latvia's defense ministry.
For its part, Ukraine has increasingly targeted warehouses belonging to Russia's biggest online retailer Wildberries, saying the company supplies components for Russian drones.
Near Moscow, another Wildberries warehouse was set ablaze by Ukrainian drones overnight. Since mid-July, Ukraine has struck around 20 warehouses and buildings linked to the company.
Zelensky says those strikes, along with attacks on oil refineries, are aimed at undermining Russia's war economy.
In July alone, 437 civilians were killed in Ukraine, the highest monthly toll since May 2022, according to a United Nations tally. Russian authorities separately reported 79 civilians killed on their side in July, up from the previous month.

articles.title: Poland Begins Developing Long-Range Strike Capabilities Beyond 1,000 km
articles.body:
Poland aims to develop the capability to conduct precision strikes against targets more than 1,000 kilometers away. The country is considering strike drones, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles as potential weapons.
Brigadier General Grzegorz Potrzuski, Head of the Planning and Programming Directorate for the Development of the Polish Armed Forces, said this in an interview with Defence24.
According to Potrzuski, Poland’s land forces can currently strike ground targets at ranges of around 300 kilometers using U.S.-made ATACMS and South Korean CTM-290 missiles. However, the experience of the Russia-Ukraine war has shown the need for precision-strike weapons capable of reaching much greater distances.
In addition to ground-based systems, the Polish Armed Forces will also receive long-range air-launched cruise missiles. In May 2024, Poland’s Ministry of National Defence signed a contract for the delivery of several hundred U.S.-made AGM-158 JASSM-ER air-to-surface cruise missiles.
The contract is reportedly worth approximately $735 million. Deliveries are scheduled to take place from 2026 to 2030.
The AGM-158 JASSM-ER has a range of up to 1,000 kilometers and carries a 450 kg warhead. The missile uses GPS guidance, while during the terminal phase of flight, it employs an infrared seeker to locate and acquire the target.
According to the brigadier general, the General Staff of the Polish Armed Forces is already working on a doctrine for conducting deep precision strikes. The doctrine is intended to establish the principles for developing the required capabilities and to define requirements for the Polish defense industry regarding future weapon systems for the Polish Armed Forces.
To carry out these missions, Poland does not plan to create additional military units. Instead, specialized units will be established within existing structures, with their capabilities gradually expanded until they reach full operational readiness.
One of the first steps in developing Poland’s domestic missile industry is expected to be the establishment of a joint venture to produce CGR-080 rockets, with a range of approximately 80 kilometers, for the Homar-K multiple launch rocket system (MLRS).
Over the next several years, Polish companies are expected to master their production and establish a technological foundation for the further development of the country’s missile capabilities.
Meanwhile, Poland is assessing the availability and development potential of strike UAVs, cruise missiles, and ballistic missiles. The country may pursue these projects independently or in cooperation with foreign allies.
According to the general, in addition to developing strike capabilities, Poland also needs to strengthen its intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance capabilities required to detect targets, determine their coordinates, and assess the results of strikes.

articles.title: Ukraine could launch ballistic missiles in three months, former defense minister says
articles.body:
Ukraine could strike Russia with domestically produced ballistic missiles within the next few months, the country’s former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov told CBS on Sunday.
Fedorov, who was recently ousted by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, said that Ukraine could be able to launch the missiles within three to six months' time
"We need to defeat Russia in every technological cycle, and we have to make decisions 24/7," he told CBS.
Fedorov has often been credited with being the architect of Ukraine’s current war strategy. While he noted that it would be difficult to predict exactly when Ukrainian ballistic missiles would be deployed, he emphasized that Ukraine has “no choice but to do it.”
In June, Ukrainian defense company Fire Point began testing a ballistic model, which would allow Kyiv to respond to Moscow’s attacks. Fire Point has also said that it aims to begin launching interceptor missiles, but they will likely not be available until 2027.
While it is on the uptick, Ukraine struggles to intercept Russian ballistic missiles because of its mass interceptor shortage.
Zelensky: If the US sells us 10% of Patriot missiles, 'we will destroy all the Russians' ballistic missiles'
On Sunday evening, the Ukrainian Air Force was unable to intercept any of the ballistic missiles that Russia fired at the country.
As such, Ukraine has mainly relied on long-range drones and cruise missiles to attack Russia.
Zelensky has been publicly pleading with the US and Europe for more interceptor missiles. In an interview with CNN, he said he has only about 10% of the interceptor missiles he needs.
If the US “sells us 5%, we will go through the winter and save people’s lives. If they can sell us 10%, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1%,” he said.
After Trump walked back his public commitment to give Ukraine the Patriot missile interceptors, representatives from Lockheed Martin, which produces the Patriots, went to Kyiv to start discussions. But even if Ukraine does get the license, it would take at least a year, if not more, to produce them.
Ukraine has notably been receiving even fewer Patriot missiles than before due to the US interceptor shortage that stemmed from the war with Iran.
“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky told CNN, regarding the interceptors.
“I don’t have 5% now, and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me a big challenge, one of the biggest I have had from the very beginning of this war.”
In response, a White House official told CNN that the Pentagon “is currently exploring several potential pathways for future defense industrial cooperation with Ukraine.
“These discussions are in the exploratory phase; no specific industrial cooperation initiatives have been decided upon or guaranteed at this stage,” the official added.
“We must prioritize protecting these exquisite systems and expanding overall production of critical weapons systems for the US warfighter and for our partners and allies.”
Zelensky also told CNN that he would not concede any territory in Ukraine’s Donbas region, which Russia has repeatedly sought to control.
“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory,” he said.
“The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why will he not come again to occupy us?”
He then signaled that he agreed with some assessments that Putin could try to expand the war in Ukraine to take on NATO.
“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society,” he said.
“It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in NATO or not in NATO. He wants quick victory, 100% sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”

articles.title: Ukrainian Navy Strikes Bastion Missile System Positions in Crimea
articles.body:
In the early hours of August 16, Ukrainian Navy units struck the launch positions and deployment site of a Bastion coastal missile system in temporarily occupied Crimea.
The video of the strike was released by the Ukrainian Navy press service.
Judging by the released video, FP-2 drones were used in the strike. According to the General Staff, the strike took place near the village of Rezervne, not far from Sevastopol.
The Navy said the strike caused significant losses in equipment and personnel. The final extent of the enemy’s losses is still being determined.
The Bastion system was originally intended to engage surface ships, but Russia uses it to strike ground targets in Ukraine with P-800 Oniks and 3M22 Zircon missiles.
The system is produced in two variants: the mobile Bastion-P and the stationary, or silo-based, Bastion-S, with the latter primarily intended for export. Each Bastion-P launcher carries two missiles in transport-launch containers for vertical launch.
The Oniks anti-ship missile is 8.9 meters long and has a diameter of 0.7 meters. Its launch weight is 3 tons, and its wingspan is 1.7 meters. The high-explosive penetrating warhead weighs 300 kg. The engine allows the missile to reach a maximum speed of up to Mach 2.6, or 3,182 km/h, at high altitude, and about Mach 2, or 2,448 km/h, near the surface.
Thanks to their supersonic speed and ability to fly at extremely low altitudes, missiles of this type are difficult targets to intercept. Russian forces typically use them to strike Odesa and coastal areas.
The 3M22 Zircon anti-ship missile was developed for use with the 3S14 universal vertical launch system installed on ships, but was later adapted for launch from ground-based systems.
The missile’s exact specifications are unknown. By studying fragments of downed missiles, Ukrainian researchers have established that the warhead weighs approximately 150-200 kg, of which about 40-80 kg is explosive.
According to the latest research, the Zircon is likely not a hypersonic cruise missile but rather a ballistic missile that uses a quasi-ballistic trajectory.
For more details about the system, see our special report, “Russia’s Bastion: Threat to Ukraine and the Capabilities of the Missile System.“

articles.title: Over 1,550 Drones, 62 Missiles Target Ukraine in One Week
articles.body:
Russian forces launched over 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 aerial bombs, and 62 missiles – primarily ballistic – at Ukraine over the past week, President Volodymyr Zelensky stated on Sunday, Aug. 16.
In a statement on Telegram, Zelensky highlighted the scale of the attacks, which targeted 13 regions across the country.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He provided an update on the casualties from recent strikes, reporting that two people were killed and 14 injured in Kryvyi Rih, while one person was killed in Sumy. In Kyiv and the surrounding region, six people were injured.
Zelensky added that Russian forces also struck Kremenchuk with ballistic missiles, stating that civilian infrastructure is targeted wherever Russian ballistic capabilities can reach. Emergency services are working to eliminate fires and conduct rescue operations at the strike sites.
The president used the update to reiterate calls for international partners to supply Ukraine with air defense systems.
“When North Korean ballistic missiles destroy infrastructure and take lives here in Europe, European interceptors cannot simply remain in warehouses,” Zelensky said. “Protecting lives is necessary. Russia must be stopped. New packages mean literally saved lives and protected infrastructure every day.”
Domestic production and air defense needs
Zelensky’s remarks follow an address on Friday, Aug. 14, in which he discussed Ukraine’s efforts to secure air defense missiles and agreements for domestic weapons production.
Ukraine Tests Last Shadow T200 Interceptor Drone, Exceeding Expected Range
In that address, Zelensky stated that the government is working to acquire additional anti-ballistic capabilities and Patriot systems. He also noted that Ukraine is seeking production licenses for anti-ballistic capabilities and expanded contributions to the PURL weapons-purchasing program.
The president pointed to the acquisition of F-16 fighter jets and the domestic production of drones as evidence that Ukraine can achieve its defense goals. However, he warned that political delays in supplying weapons carry a human cost.
“Every delay, which unfortunately exists at the political level, simply takes lives,” Zelensky said.

articles.title: The Iran War Toll
articles.body:
Trump’s war with Iran:
- Rallied the Iranian nation behind the regime and took oxygen away from the opposition, which had appeared to have the unpopular regime on the ropes earlier in the year with its demonstrations - perhaps by honoring pledges to support those demonstrating back in January 2026, lives could have been saved. As was, people seem to have died in vain.
- Failed at its initial aim for regime change but resulted in installing a new, more radical and uncompromising leadership in Iran, bent on revenge against the US and its allies
- Failed to completely take out Iran’s nuclear program, but perhaps made the regime more likely to go nuclear in the end. Maintaining a program on the threshold of going nuclear but not, failed to act as a deterrent but instead got the regime attacked. Perhaps the message is that only states armed with nukes are safe from attack, and the message to others is to proliferate. The irony is the intervention was aimed at countering nuclear proliferation, but it may well have the opposite effect.
- By making the war existential in talking about regime change it reduced the bar for the regime to escalate with attacks on Gulf states and closing the Straits. In so doing it has gifted the regime a new deterrence - its ability to cripple the Gulf states, the Straits and the global economy through the use of cheap/low tech drones and missiles;
- Through its control of the Straits, Iran is likely now to be able to toll/levy charges for passage, generating revenues for the regime. Prior to the war, the Straits offered free passage.
- Likely the Trump administration will cede a deal to Iran which eases sanctions, eases asset freezes and generates investment flows to further sustain the regime;
- Pushed oil and energy prices higher, stalling global growth and boosting inflation. Higher inflation will stall policy rate cuts, keeping rates higher for longer, further stalling global growth. Global GDP is going to be lower, meaning the global population is collectively poorer.
- Drawn-down global strategic oil reserves are increasing the chances of a systemic global shock in the future.
- Resulted in higher oil and energy prices, which boosted revenues to axis of evil states - Russia, Iran et al. Likely, they bolstered the Russian budget just at the time when in late 2025/early 2026 sanctions were beginning to impact with the Urals oil price discount running at one-third in the early part of 26’, the budget deficit by the end of February at the full year target with Urals down around the 40s a barrel. By bolstering Russia’s fiscal and BOP position it has extended the duration of the war in Ukraine, causing more deaths.
- The war has depleted finite stocks of critical US missiles, including Patriots and THAADs. These are expensive and time-consuming to replace and are now leaving Ukraine short of air defenses, and encouraging Putin to launch ballistic missile attacks and extend the war. The shortage of air defense missiles leaves the Gulf and the US vulnerable and Taiwan open to attack by China.
- The war has shown the limits of US military power and exposed a failure to learn from the recent conflict in Ukraine in the use of drones and military technology. The war will encourage enemies of the US, including China, which had already invested heavily in drone tech.
- The war has left the impression that the US is an unreliable partner and has furthered efforts by key allies to diversify defense ties away from the US This was seen this week with the signing of the Mecca Agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan. By such states hedging their bets this weakens US global leverage. Likely we will see similar efforts from allies in Europe – longer term this likely weakens the US network of global alliances and reduces long-term demand for US military kit - as countries move to develop autonomous military industrial capability which could ultimately serve as competition to US product.
- With the aim of diversifying away from the US, the Iran war will likely further the flight from the US dollar and US risk free assets. Nervousness around the latter move was probably highlighted by the US Treasury move to support the JPY, for fear of forced Japanese selling of US assets.
- The war has made a lasting peace in Gaza, the West Bank and even Lebanon appear less likely as suspicions on US and Israeli policy in the region have grown. It has made an extension of the Abraham Accords less likely.
- The war has further undermined US popular support for Israel and likely raises questions over the prior unlimited military and financial backing of Israel by the US.

articles.title: Ukraine launches one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, killing at least 6 people in Russia
articles.body:
Ukraine launches one of its largest aerial attacks of the war, killing at least 6 people in Russia
Ukraine launched hundreds of drones across Russia on Sunday, killing at least six people in one of Kyiv’s largest aerial attacks of the war.
Kyiv has stepped up its attacks on Russia this year, with long-range missiles and swarms of drones targeting military industries and energy facilities. It has also increasingly pummeled giant Wildberries depots, burning billions of dollars’ worth of merchandise belonging to the Russian online retail giant. Those attacks have brought the war home to the Russian public nearly 4½ years into Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Meanwhile, Ukraine also came under Russian attack, with drone strikes destroying homes and torching Kyiv’s landmark book market.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said it had destroyed 822 Ukrainian drones overnight. Some 600 drones were detected headed toward the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said, with a third of those destroyed over the Moscow region itself.
An 83-year-old man was killed after a Ukrainian drone hit a private home in the Moscow region, local Gov. Andrey Vorobyov said. He also confirmed that a Ukrainian attack had sparked a blaze at a Wildberries warehouse in the town of Podolsk.
A drone attack targeted three towns in Russia’s southwestern Rostov region, killing five people, local Gov. Yury Slyusar said. The attack, with more than 150 drones, damaged several homes and a railway station and sparked a forest fire.
Russian strikes kill 5 in Ukraine
A Russian missile attack on Ukraine’s Kryvyi Rih killed two people and wounded 14 others, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy wrote on social media Sunday. He also said that one more person had been killed in the city of Sumy.
ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine’s largest steel producer, confirmed that one of its sites had been hit in a missile attack and that operations had been partially suspended.
Elsewhere, a man and a woman died when their home was hit by a Russian strike in Ukraine’s southern Zaporizhzhia region, said Ivan Fedorov, the head of the local military administration.
Russian attacks also sparked fires throughout the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, wounding six people. A blaze took hold at one of the city’s largest book markets, tearing through kiosks huddled close to the Pochaina metro station. Firefighters fought back the flames, which sent plumes of black smoke across the capital, and picked their way through rubble where the market’s crowded pavilions once stood.
“Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” Zelenskyy said.
Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Sunday that it had targeted a metallurgical plant in Kryvyi Rih and several military-industrial sites in Kyiv, including a manufacturing facility for Ukraine’s Flamingo missiles.
The domestically produced missiles are increasingly key to Ukraine’s long-range attacks on Russia, with Zelenskyy announcing Saturday that Kyiv had used the weapons to attack a rocket research and production center in Samara approximately 900 kilometers (560 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
NATO jet downs drone in Romanian airspace
Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said Sunday that a Spanish Air and Space Force F-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered Romanian airspace.
The drone’s entry into the NATO member’s airspace was detected by surveillance systems at 4:44 a.m., the ministry said, about 24 kilometers (14.9 miles) north of the eastern city of Galati near the border with neighboring Moldova. Moldova is a landlocked country between Ukraine and Romania.
A Spanish F-18 aircraft that was performing air policing duties “made radar contact with the target and received engagement approval,” the ministry said. “The drone was safely shot down by the F-18 aircraft at 05:01.”
The ministry later said that drone debris was also reported in the Black Sea around 10 a.m. on Sunday, about 1.5 kilometers (0.9 miles) from the coastal city of Constanta.
Officials did not specify the drone’s origin.
The incident comes weeks after Romanian pilots shot down three drones over three days as Russia intensified attacks against Ukraine near the border. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Romania has reported dozens of drone incidents, including some that have crashed and exploded on its territory.
Acting Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said in a post on X that the Spanish deployment in Romania was scaled up “at the request of Romania and NATO to bolster the Eastern Flank following prior drone incidents,” and that it was Spain’s fourth such deployment.

articles.title: One alternative to air defense: Ukraine strikes Russian Bastion system used to attack Ukrainian cities from Crimea
articles.body:
Ukraine’s Navy said its forces struck the launch positions and deployment site of a Russian Bastion coastal missile system in occupied Crimea overnight on 16 August, reportedly inflicting significant losses in equipment and personnel.
Russia has regularly used Crimea as a launch platform for strikes against Ukraine, making its missile systems there a priority target for Ukrainian forces seeking to reduce Russia’s ability to attack Ukrainian territory.
The Navy said the final Russian losses were still being assessed and did not provide details on the weapons or personnel destroyed.
Bastion systems used to strike Ukraine
The Bastion is a costly and scarce Russian coastal missile system that can launch P-800 Oniks cruise missiles. Russia has used Oniks missiles launched from occupied Crimea to attack targets across southern and other regions of Ukraine.
Oniks is a supersonic anti-ship cruise missile that Russia has adapted for strikes against ground targets in Ukraine, including Odesa Oblast. The missile can travel at more than 3,000 km/h, making it difficult for air defenses to intercept. Its standard range is about 300 kilometers, while upgraded variants can reportedly reach up to 800 kilometers and carry a 300-kilogram warhead. Russia launches ground attacks with Oniks from mobile Bastion systems based in occupied Crimea.
The Navy also said Russia uses Bastion systems to launch Zircon hypersonic missiles against Ukraine.
The Zircon is a newer hypersonic cruise missile designed to reach speeds of roughly Mach 5–9. Russia has used it against Ukrainian cities, including Kyiv, with launches previously reported from Bastion systems in occupied Crimea. Its officially claimed range exceeds 1,000 kilometers, although analysts question that figure; Ukrainian analysts have estimated a lower effective range.
Bastion launchers in Crimea are a particularly important target for Ukraine: they give Russia a mobile platform for striking targets across southern Ukraine and, with Zircon, deep into the country. Ukraine’s air defenses have struggled to intercept these missiles, making strikes on the launchers an important way to reduce the threat before the missiles are fired.
The Ukrainian Navy said the strike was part of ongoing efforts to reduce Russia’s combat potential in the Black Sea region.
Several Ukrainian strikes recorded overnight
The Crimea strike came amid a broader wave of Ukrainian attacks on Russian military, industrial, and logistics targets overnight on 16 August.
Ukraine’s General Staff reported a strike on the Kamensky Combine in Russia’s Rostov Oblast, where a fire was recorded. The plant produces solid rocket fuel for Russia’s Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, as well as components for other missile and aviation weapons.
In Moscow Oblast, a Ukrainian drone struck a 250,000-square-meter Wildberries warehouse in Koledino, while another fire was reported at the Severnoye Domodedovo logistics complex. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry later confirmed the Wildberries facility had been put out of operation, saying it was the retailer’s largest warehouse by area.
The General Staff also confirmed the results of two earlier strikes. It said the ZapSibNeftekhim petrochemical complex in Tobolsk was shut down after its central gas-fractionation unit was struck on 10 August, while an 11 August strike damaged several processing units at the Orsknaftaorgsyntez refinery in Orenburg Oblast.
The strikes show the expanding reach of Ukraine’s campaign against the military and industrial infrastructure supporting Russia’s war, from missile systems and rocket-fuel production to oil, petrochemical, and logistics facilities.

articles.title: ‘Massive’ Ukrainian drone attack on Russia kills at least six, says Moscow
articles.body:
Ukraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities.
Russia’s defence ministry said it had shot down 822 drones, while the mayor of Moscow, Sergei Sobyanin, reported that 600 drones were launched towards the capital’s region, of which 201 were destroyed.
It was the biggest air raid on the Russian capital in two years, the mayor told the Tass news agency, although the rapid recent expansion of Ukraine’s drone’s capability could mean it was the largest attack wave since the start of the war in 2022.
Russian drone missile attacks killed seven people in Ukraine, including two in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed the border into Romania.
The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said.
A warehouse belonging to the Russian distribution company Wildberries was set on fire in Podolsk, south of Moscow, with photographs showing a blaze apparently engulfing the 200,000 sq metre warehouse and black smoke extending into the sky.
Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory” – and the Russian defence ministry said later that it had shot down nine Ukrainian cruise missiles and 1,478 drones in the previous 24 hours, though the figure could not be independently verified.
Ukraine has rapidly expanded its long-range, deep-strike missile and drone capabilities in 2026, allowing it to attack warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities at distances of up to 1,500 miles (2,400km) from its border.
That has allowed Ukraine to nearly match the long-range strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war, at a time when both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion.
Over the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to the Wildberries company, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukrainian attacks have struck about 20 warehouses and buildings in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially.
Five people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine. Its governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. One person was reported dead in the attacks on the Moscow area.
Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital.
Fire caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the blaze.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media posting.
Over the past week, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs, and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities, most of them ballistic missiles of various types.
Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down.

articles.title: Ukraine Hits Russia’s Bastion Launch Sites in Crimea Used to Fire Oniks and Zircon Missiles
articles.body:

Ukraine Hits Russia’s Bastion Launch Sites in Crimea Used to Fire Oniks and Zircon Missiles
Ukrainian forces struck Russian Bastion coastal missile positions in temporarily occupied Crimea overnight on August 16, targeting launch sites and a deployment area for a system Russia uses to fire Oniks and Zircon missiles against Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Ukraine’s Navy said on August 16 that the strike caused significant losses in Russian weapons and personnel, adding that the full extent of the damage was still being assessed. The Navy described the Bastion as a scarce and costly missile system used by Russian forces to strike southern and other regions of Ukraine with supersonic Oniks and hypersonic Zircon missiles.
The K-300P Bastion is a road-mobile coastal defense system originally developed to engage surface ships. A standard launcher carries two P-800 Oniks missiles, allowing the battery to relocate between firing positions and launch from prepared or temporary sites.
The Oniks travels at more than twice the speed of sound and can carry a warhead weighing up to around 300 kilograms.
Russia has also adapted the Bastion infrastructure for strikes involving the 3M22 Zircon, according to the Ukrainian Navy. Zircon was originally developed as a ship- and submarine-launched hypersonic anti-ship missile.
Russian specifications claim speeds of up to Mach 9 and a range of around 1,000 kilometers, although its actual battlefield performance has been subject to scrutiny following its use against Ukraine.
The strike came hours after Russia again used Oniks missiles against Ukraine. During the overnight attack on August 16, Russian forces targeted Kyiv, Kremenchuk and Kryvyi Rih with Oniks missiles, Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles, Kh-59/69 guided missiles and 106 drones, according to Ukraine’s Air Force.
Ukrainian defenses downed or suppressed three Kh-59/69 missiles and 85 drones, while impacts were recorded at 13 locations. The Air Force did not specify the number or launch location of the Oniks missiles, so they cannot be directly linked to the Bastion positions struck in Crimea.
Russia has repeatedly used Oniks and Zircon missiles during large-scale attacks on Ukrainian cities. On August 5, Russian forces launched four Zircon or Oniks missiles alongside 24 Iskander-M/S-400 ballistic missiles and 115 drones, with Kyiv and the surrounding region as the main target.
The attack killed 17 people and injured 44, while damaging civilian businesses, logistics facilities and railway infrastructure.
Ukraine has previously targeted Russia’s Bastion capability in temporarily occupied Crimea. On March 24, the General Staff reported that Ukrainian forces struck a Bastion launcher along with other Russian military targets.
The strikes come as Russia continues expanding production of both missile types. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence (HUR) said on August 10 that Russia produced 33 Zircon and 60 Oniks missiles during the first seven months of 2026, already meeting its annual production targets for both weapons.

articles.title: Russia, Ukraine report casualties in overnight drone, missile strikes
articles.body:
Elena Teslova
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
At least seven people were killed and 13 injured in Ukrainian drone attacks across Russia, while three people were killed and 23 injured in Russian strikes across Ukraine, officials on both sides said Sunday.
 
Rostov region Governor Yury Slyusar said in a statement on Russian social media platform Max that five civilians were killed in Ukrainian drone attacks as more than 150 drones were destroyed over three cities and nine districts of the region.
 
“The death toll from the enemy’s night attack has risen -- two more people have been found dead. They were discovered by rescuers. I express my deepest condolences to the families and loved ones of the victims,” he said.
 
Slyusar added that multiple residential buildings and civilian infrastructure were damaged in the attack.
 
In a separate statement, Moscow region Governor Andrey Vorobyov said an 83-year-old man was killed when a drone fell on a private house in the Ramensky municipal district.
 
Meanwhile, acting Belgorod region Governor Aleksandr Shuvayev said a Ukrainian drone struck a bus carrying workers, killing a woman and injuring nine people.
 
Separately, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said around 600 drones had flown toward Moscow overnight, making it the largest attack on the capital in more than two years.
 
“The Defense Ministry air defense systems shot down nine more drones attacking Moscow. Three people in the area of the Moscow Ring Road were injured,” he said.
 
For his part, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on Telegram that two people were killed in Kryvyi Rih and another in Sumy, while six people were injured in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
 
“In Kryvyi Rih, two people died and 14 others were injured. There is one death in Sumy,” he said.
 
Earlier, the head of the Kryvyi Rih administration had reported one death and 13 injuries, indicating that casualty figures were still being updated.
 
Ukraine also continued strikes on Wildberries warehouses, with Vorobyov saying on Max that another facility caught fire at the Koledino industrial park in the city of Podolsk following a drone attack.
 
The attack also left 110 residential homes without electricity, according to Grigory Artamonov, head of the Podolsk urban district.
 
A separate logistics facility used to store medicines in Domodedovo caught fire and partially collapsed, with the damaged area estimated at 56,000 square meters (602,779 square feet), local authorities said.
 
More than 150 flights were either delayed or canceled at three Moscow airports -- Sheremetyevo, Vnukovo and Domodedovo -- amid the Ukrainian drone attack.
 
Both the Russian Defense Ministry and Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed carrying out overnight attacks.
 
The Russian Defense Ministry said its forces carried out a group strike using precision weapons and long-range drones against Ukrainian defense-industrial facilities in Kyiv, the Kremenchuk oil refinery in the Poltava region and metallurgical facilities in Kryvyi Rih.
 
The ministry said Kyiv-based enterprises produced components for Ukraine’s long-range Flamingo missiles and drones, while the Kryvyi Rih metallurgical complex produced steel for weapons and military equipment.
 
It also said a cargo ship carrying military supplies for Ukrainian forces was hit at the port of Odesa.
 
Ukraine’s General Staff, meanwhile, said its forces struck a Russian Bastion coastal missile complex in Crimea, hitting its launch positions and deployment site.
 
It added that a railway bridge near the settlement of Svitlodolynskyi in the Zaporizhzhia region was also hit.
 
Logistics and ammunition depots in Karlovka in the Donetsk region were also struck, it said.
 
Independent verification of the claims made by both sides remains difficult due to the ongoing conflict.

articles.title: Iran, US trade Hormuz threats; Hamas in Cairo for Gaza talks
articles.body:
Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in the Middle East.
Here are the key events on Sunday afternoon:
• Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya and Trump envoy Jared Kushner are in Cairo for talks with mediators over the Board of Peace's stalled Gaza plan. The two are expected to hold face-to-face talks before Kushner travels to Israel to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who last week rejected the deal to disarm Hamas.
• Iran and the US are continuing to sabre-rattle over the Strait of Hormuz. Trump on Saturday claimed he could declare the strategic waterway a "territory of the United States" while a senior Iranian diplomat told the US to "accept the reality of defeat".
• The threats come ahead of Monday's deadline under the June Islamabad agreement, which gave the US and Iran two months to reach an understanding on reopening the key waterway.
• Iran's foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said talks with Oman over the strait are continuing but that re-opening the waterway is a "completely separate matter" that will depend on the US meeting Tehran's conditions.
• Qatar has denied claims by Iran that it is holding three pilots captured during a combat mission earlier in the war.
• Israel has threatened to further escalate attacks on Lebanon, a day after killing at least 11 people in one of the heaviest rounds of strikes since the ceasefire came into effect in June.
President Donald Trump's son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner will meet in Egypt with Hamas leadership as he pushes a peace plan, sources from Hamas told AFP on Sunday.
"Mediators informed Hamas that US envoy Jared Kushner will hold a meeting with the Hamas leadership, in the presence of Egyptian and Qatari officials, before Kushner travels to Israel to meet Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu," said one of the Hamas sources, requesting anonymity to discuss the sensitive diplomacy.
Iran offers $30,000 bounty for killing, capturing US troops
Iran's military announced on Sunday that it was offering a bounty equivalent to $30,000 for killing or capturing US soldiers, with the reward doubled if carried out by a woman.
Army chief Amir Hatami said the plan had been drawn up following "the large number of requests" to participate in the financial support, according to the IRNA state news agency.
There has been no known deployment of US ground forces in Iran during the Middle East war, with the exception of a rescue mission in April for a downed American pilot.
Hatami did not provide any details on where or when the killing or capturing of US soldiers was expected to take place.
"Anyone who kills or captures and hands over an invading American military personnel will receive a reward equivalent to $30,000 or 5 billion tomans from the Islamic Republic of Iran's Army," Hatami said, using an informal unit equivalent to 10,000 Iranian rials.
"Courageous Iranian women who carry out such an action will receive double the reward," he added.
US President Donald Trump's envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner talked with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi on Sunday about the implementation of the Gaza ceasefire, Sisi's spokesperson said.
The meeting in the Mediterranean city of El-Alamein "emphasised the need for all parties to fulfill their obligations under the Gaza Strip ceasefire agreement", spokesperson Mohamed El-Shennawy said in a statement.
Kushner is in Egypt at the same time as a Hamas delegation led by its leader Khalil al-Hayya, who met with Egypt's intelligence chief Hassan Rashad on Sunday morning.
Kushner speaks at the inaugural Board of Peace meeting on 19 February 2026. [Getty]
Iranian govt votes to further criminalise 'hostile media'
Iran's parliament approved a bill on Sunday that would criminalise interviews and other communications with media deemed hostile to the Islamic Republic, including US or Israeli media and outlets financed by either country, Iran's Shargh newspaper reported.
Under the bill, which must still be reviewed by the Guardian Council before it can become law, interviews or participation in discussions with such media would be banned and violations punishable by six months to two years in prison.
Interviews with other foreign media would require notification to the intelligence ministry, while contact with foreign embassies, offices of foreign organisations or other non-Iranian institutions without notification and written permission from the foreign ministry would be punishable by a fine and deprivation of certain social rights.
The bill would also harden penalties for economic crimes committed under the direction or supervision of foreigners, ban providing information to foreigners without intelligence ministry approval and restrict scientific cooperation with foreign institutions outside an approved list.
It would punish policy or legislative proposals made under the direction of foreign intelligence services if they harm Iran's security or independence, with prison terms of up to 30 years. Cases would be heard by Revolutionary Courts.
Pope Leo called on Sunday for an end to violence against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank, amid a surge of attacks by settlers and a siege in the territory's village of Qusra.
Israeli settlers encircled houses after cutting off water and electricity, in what rights groups have said is a concerted effort to seize more land, and further eat into territory where Palestinians aim to establish a state.
"I renew my appeal for an end to the repeated violence against the Palestinian civilian population in the West Bank," the Pope said, without mentioning specific confrontations or attacks.
"I urgently ask the international community to take action so as to advance the two-state solution, for a fair and lasting peace," the Pope added after noon prayers at his Castel Gandolfo residence outside Rome.
The Vatican has long backed the idea of a future Palestinian state, which has been recognised by more than 150 of 193 UN member states as encompassing the Gaza Strip and West Bank, including East Jerusalem.
Hamas delegation, Egypt spy chief hold talks on Gaza plan
A Hamas delegation met Egyptian intelligence chief Hassan Rashad on Sunday to discuss ways to advance the implementation of a post-war plan for Gaza, Egypt's state news agency reported.
The Middle East News Agency said the delegation led by Hamas chief Khalil al-Hayya "reaffirmed commitment to completing US President Donald Trump's plan".
Hamas had said in late July that it was ready to hand over its weapons to a nascent technical committee set to govern Gaza, as part of a 15-point plan announced by Trump's Board of Peace.
But Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the plan, vowing there would be no withdrawal of Israeli forces from Gaza until the full disarmament of Hamas.
The delegation arrived in Egypt on Saturday evening, ahead of a visit by Trump's envoy Jared Kushner to the region.
Palestinian child killed by Israeli forces in Gaza
The Palestinian Red Crescent on Sunday recovered the body of 14-year-old near Khan Younis in southern Gaza, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.
Suhail Masoud Shalouf was shot by Israeli forces on Saturday evening on al-Tina Street, south of Khan Younis.
Meanwhile, medics said three Palestinians were wounded by Israeli gunfire after Israeli forces targeted tents in the Al-Mawasi displacement camp, west of Khan Younis.
UK minister condemns West Bank 'settler terrorism'
UK Middle East Minister Stephen Doughty has condemned the ongoing wave of settler violence in the occupied West Bank
"I am horrified at the scenes we are seeing yet again in recent days in the West Bank and the shocking surge in settler violence," he said in a video statement on X.
"Settler violence and settler terrorism are appalling and must end," he said, calling on the Israeli government to prevent further anti-Palestinian violence.
Doughty's comments came on the back of international outrage at the besieging of Palestinians in the village of Qusra, where the Israeli military enabled a days-long siege of civilian homes by settler militants.
Hamas chief in Cairo for Gaza talks ahead of Kushner visit
Hamas political chief Khalil al-Hayya in in Cairo for talks with Egyptian officials ahead of a visit by US President Donald Trump's envoy Jared Kushner to the region.
Hayya, who is visiting Egypt for the first time since assuming leadership of Hamas in late July, was expected to meet with Egypt's intelligence chief Hassan Rashad on Sunday morning, the source said.
Kushner will visit Israel and Egypt next week in a bid to rescue the Trump-backed Board of Peace's Gaza plan rejected by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
He will be accompanied by Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's Gaza envoy.
Yemeni government forces said Sunday that Houthi fighters have launched new missile and drone attacks on the port city of Mocha.
Air defences had intercepted a drone fired by the group, they said.
The director of Mocha port said Saturday it has been forced to suspend operations after being hit by more than 25 missiles in recent days.
The recent attacks have raised fears that Yemen could be sliding back into civil war, four years after a ceasefire ended the conflict between the Iran-aligned Houthis and the Saudi-backed, internationally-recognised government.
The head of Iran's parliamentary national security committee, Ebrahim Azizi, has mocked Trump over his latest threats to take over the Strait of Hormuz.
"The US President ought to worry about his own security rather than his endless bluffing regarding the Strait of Hormuz; before he ends up hiding in a food truck," Azizi wrote on X on Saturday.
He was referring to reports in US media that Trump hid in a catering truck to leave Air Force One during a recent visit to Turkey following concerns about an Iranian attack.
Iran executes man over involvement in January protests
Iran's judiciary announced the execution on Sunday of a man who was convicted of running over several police officers with his car during anti-government protests in January.
"Shahram Sadeghi, sentenced to death for having carried out an operational action in support of the Zionist regime and the United States, was executed this morning," the judiciary's Mizan Online website said.
It added that the man had run over several police officers with his car on 8 January in Karaj, west of Tehran, wounding seven of them.
A protest movement initially sparked in late December by the high cost of living rapidly evolved into widespread anti-government demonstrations that peaked on 8 and 9 January.
Israel threatens escalation in Lebanon amid new strike
Lebanese media reported a new Israeli attack in the south on Sunday shortly after Israel's defence minister Israel Katz vowed to continue strikes.
Lebanon's National News Agency reported in a strike in Majdal Zoun on Sunday morning, a day after at least 11 people were killed in the heaviest Israeli attacks since the US-brokered ceasefire came into effect in June.
"No account in any arena will remain open. We will defend our soldiers and civilians with force," Katz wrote on X.
Medics at the site of an Israeli strike in Deir al-Zahrani, 15 August 2026. [Getty]
Iran disputes Qatar, Kuwait accounts of captured pilots
An Iranian military official said on Sunday that Qatar should allow an Iranian team to enter the country to investigate the fate of pilots whom Tehran says were captured by Qatari forces, Iranian media reported.
Qatar denies holding any Iranian pilots. Doha said on Saturday that its search and rescue teams had found the remains of one pilot after Iranian aircraft violated Qatari airspace in March and failed to respond to attempts to contact them.
Qatar said it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of the remains and had invited Tehran to review details of its search and rescue operations, but had received no response.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran's Armed Forces General Staff, said an Iranian Air Force expert and fact-finding team had been waiting for months to enter Qatar, according to the semi-official Tasnim news agency.
He accused Qatari officials of repeatedly delaying the investigation and preventing the pilots' return to Iran. He called for the International Committee of the Red Cross to urgently follow up on the case.

articles.title: Iran, US trade threats; Israel threatens to escalate in Lebanon
articles.body:

A woman was killed and six people were wounded in a missile and drone attack on Kryvyi Rih, the hometown of President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in central Ukraine, the region’s governor said.

Defence and foreign policy analyst Pavel Felgenhauer told Al Jazeera that the targeting of capital cities suggests an escalation in the war.
