articles.title: U.S. Air Force buys Chinese-made drones for nuclear missile base
articles.body:
- The U.S. Air Force is buying DJI drones for F.E. Warren AFB to train missile security forces against the type of foreign drones they are most likely to encounter.
- The brand-name justification cites DJI's 80 to 85 percent global market share and says the drones will run modified "RIZER" software to block data transfer before use.
The U.S. Air Force is buying Chinese-made DJI drones for a Wyoming nuclear missile base, using the foreign aircraft as stand-ins for the kind of drones security forces there are training to detect and shoot down.
The 90th Contracting Squadron posted a combined synopsis and solicitation on August 14 seeking a small business vendor to supply the drones for F.E. Warren Air Force Base, home to the 90th Missile Security Operations Squadron and part of Air Force Global Strike Command. Quotes are due August 24, with questions due five days earlier. The squadron says it needs the aircraft to run counter-small unmanned aircraft systems training, exercises meant to test radar, jamming and other defeat systems against real drone signals rather than simulated ones.
The order calls for two DJI Mavic 2 Pro quadcopters with Fly More kits, listed as refurbished, two DJI Mini 3 Pro drones with remote controllers, two DJI Avata 2 Fly More combos and six airdrop payload release devices, plus shipping. The government intends to award a firm fixed price contract to the lowest-priced offer that meets the technical requirements, according to the solicitation.
Contracting officials designated the purchase a brand-name requirement, meaning DJI specifically, rather than an open competition among drone makers. A justification document signed July 29 by Contracting Officer Chad A. Evans, a technical sergeant, states that DJI controls an estimated 80 to 85 percent of the global commercial drone market and that its “highly distinct, proprietary electronic protocols, radio frequency (RF) signatures, and flight capabilities” are not replicated by American-made drones or other manufacturers.
“To properly test our counter-systems and train our operators against the most statistically probable real-world threat, the 90 MSOS must utilize the exact devices adversaries are most likely to employ,” the justification states.
The document warns that without the specific DJI hardware, the squadron’s “no-fail nuclear security mission” would be degraded. Relying only on computer-simulated data or U.S.-made drones, the justification argues, would leave operators untested against DJI’s actual radio signatures and communication protocols, creating what it calls a critical blind spot in installation defense.
F.E. Warren is one of three U.S. Air Force bases that operates Minuteman III intercontinental ballistic missiles, and its security forces are responsible for defending that missile field against ground and airborne threats. The justification states that Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana, another Global Strike Command missile base, is pursuing or using similar DJI platforms for its own counter-drone training, and frames the F.E. Warren purchase as bringing the two installations toward standardized threat replication across the command’s missile fields.
The document cites a Secretary of War memo titled “Unleashing U.S. Military Drone Dominance” as the legal authority permitting officers at the rank of O-6, or colonel, and equivalent to procure small quantities of foreign drone equipment for electronic warfare testing, training and counter-UAS development. That authority falls under 10 U.S.C. 2304(c)(1), which allows agencies to solicit from a single source under specific circumstances rather than through full and open competition.
To address cybersecurity concerns tied to Chinese-manufactured hardware, the justification says every DJI aircraft purchased will be loaded with software called RIZER before operational use. The document describes RIZER as overriding the drones’ native firmware to create what it calls “a completely air-gapped system that cannot transfer or download telemetry or imagery to foreign entities or DoW networks.”
The justification also states that the squadron identified multiple authorized DJI resellers and distributors capable of meeting the brand-name requirement, allowing the procurement to proceed as a 100 percent small business set-aside rather than a true single-source award to one company.

articles.title: Ex-Dutch ambassador to Ukraine says he did not expect relations with Russia to turn into war
articles.body:
Ex-Dutch ambassador to Ukraine says he did not expect relations with Russia to turn into war
He expressed this view in an interview with Ukrinform.
Recalling his appointment in 1992 as the first ambassador of the Netherlands to Ukraine, Serry said: "Already then I started to realize that I had been appointed to a country that would change Europe. I do not mean that in the tragic sense in which events are unfolding today, but I immediately felt that Ukraine would be of great importance for European security and that an independent Ukraine would be the best counterweight to Russian imperialism."
According to him, Ukraine's turbulent and tragic history created the conditions for the country to assert itself as an independent European state in 1991.
"I began to feel the importance of what had happened while traveling through newly independent Ukraine. I saw that it was not only in the West, where the Ukrainian national movement had traditionally been stronger, that a distinct identity existed; there was also something that united the entire country across all its regions. I must also confess that I fell a little in love with Ukraine. It is a beautiful country with enormous potential," the diplomat said.
At the same time, he admitted that he did not expect relations between Russia and Ukraine to turn into such a horrific war.
"On the contrary, those were more optimistic times, when it seemed possible to find some accommodation between Russia and Ukraine. Those were the Yeltsin years, which made it possible to address many of the problems between the Russian Federation and newly independent Ukraine. Think of the Black Sea Fleet, Crimea, and other issues that were then being dealt with through negotiations," Serry said.
According to him, the issue of the nuclear weapons left on Ukrainian territory after the collapse of the Soviet Union was a major concern for Western partners, particularly the United States, "and eventually agreements were reached on how to resolve it."
Asked whether that decision had been the right one, the diplomat said that Ukraine's options at the time had been very limited.
"First, Ukraine did not in practice control those nuclear forces, because command remained in Moscow rather than in Kyiv. Second, Ukraine’s cooperation with the West, the IMF, and the World Bank also depended on the decision to give up those weapons. All of this took place under very difficult circumstances. And here the United States played a much more important role than the European countries," Serry said.
In his opinion, the main difference between Ukraine and Russia is that after gaining independence, Ukrainians wanted to preserve it at all costs.
"In Russia, unfortunately, something very different happened: disappointment with change, because the Yeltsin period also represented the failure of Russia's economic and democratic transformation. Then Putin came with a completely different vision. And, by the way, Putin is not the only person in Russia who believes that Ukrainians are so-called 'malorosy'," Serry said.

articles.title: U.S. Navy May Redesign Ford-Class Aircraft Carriers to Suit Trump’s Preferences
articles.body:
The U.S. Navy is considering major changes to the design of its new Ford-class nuclear-powered aircraft carriers to better match President Donald Trump’s aesthetic preferences.
The Washington Post reported this, citing seven current and former U.S. officials familiar with the matter.
According to the officials, Trump wants the new carriers to look more like the warships that were in service during World War II.
The U.S. Navy is assessing whether it would make sense to move the carrier’s multi-level island, which serves as the ship’s command center, forward toward the middle of the ship. On the new Ford-class carriers, the island is located closer to the stern.
On carriers of this class, the island was moved aft to improve operational efficiency and safety. This configuration not only freed up additional deck space for aircraft operations around the catapults and reduced the time required to position aircraft for launch, but also improved landing safety by reducing turbulence in the landing area as aircraft approached the carrier.
The issue was already studied during Trump’s first term. A study conducted at the time concluded that relocating the island could cost billions of dollars and result in significant delays to the carrier program.
In addition, on August 13, Trump issued a national security memorandum directing the Navy to develop a plan to replace the highly efficient electromagnetic aircraft launch system with conventional steam catapults on future aircraft carriers. The document states that the administration favors “proven, reliable, and affordable technologies and ship designs.” Such a change could also cost billions of dollars and further exacerbate the chronic delays affecting the U.S. shipbuilding industry.
Construction of the lead Ford-class aircraft carrier, USS Gerald R. Ford, took 17 years. Three more ships of the class are currently at various stages of construction. USS John F. Kennedy is undergoing sea trials and nearing commissioning, while USS Enterprise and USS Doris Miller are under construction.
According to estimates by the U.S. Congressional Budget Office and the Navy’s latest shipbuilding plan, each future Ford-class aircraft carrier could cost approximately $22 billion.
As the publication notes, Trump has repeatedly expressed an interest in the design of U.S. Navy warships. Last year, he unveiled plans for a new class of Trump-class battleships that would lead his proposed “Golden Fleet.”
If the planned design is built, the nuclear-powered battleship, with a full-load displacement of 35,000 tons, would become the most heavily armed surface combatant ever built for the U.S. Navy.
It is planned to be equipped with surface-to-air and anti-ship missiles, land-attack missiles, hypersonic weapons, nuclear-armed cruise missiles, high-powered laser systems, and a railgun – an electromagnetic weapon.
The Congressional Budget Office estimates that building the 15 planned Trump-class battleships between 2028 and 2056 would cost approximately $275 billion. After completion of the lead ship, estimated at $23.4 billion, each subsequent ship is projected to cost about $18 billion.

articles.title: General Staff: Russia has lost 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
articles.body:
Russia has lost around 1,467,320 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Aug. 16.
The figure includes 1,510 casualties Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,270 tanks, 25,151 armored combat vehicles, 134,851 vehicles and fuel tanks, 47,007 artillery systems, 2,034 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,570 air defense systems, 439 aircraft, 354 helicopters, 463,404 unmanned aerial vehicles, 2,257 unmanned ground systems, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 to 140,000 are thought to be killed in action (KIA).
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to a lot more missing in action (MIAs). The intensity of Russian drones and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

articles.title: Spanish Hornet Shoots Down Drone Over Romania After It Entered From Moldova
articles.body:
On the night of August 16, a Spanish EF-18 fighter jet shot down a drone that had entered Romanian airspace from Moldova.
Romania’s Ministry of National Defence confirmed the incident.
The ministry’s surveillance systems detected the drone at 4:44 a.m., about 24 km (15 miles) north of the city of Galați.
A Spanish EF-18 fighter jet, deployed at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base as part of NATO’s air policing mission, established radar contact with the target and received authorization to engage it.
At 5:01 a.m., the fighter jet shot down the drone. Romania’s Ministry of National Defence said the aircraft destroyed the drone over an uninhabited area.
The possible crash site was identified between the villages of Băleni and Cudalbi in Galați County. The area is away from populated areas. Preliminary reports indicate that there were no casualties and no damage to infrastructure.
This is the fourth drone Romania has shot down in its airspace in 2026. On July 24, 25, and 26, Romanian F-16 fighter jets shot down three Russian drones after they entered Romanian airspace.
In addition, on May 19, 2026, a Romanian F-16 from the “Carpathian Vipers” unit shot down a drone in Estonian airspace. The drone had previously flown about 80 km into Estonian territory.
The handover ceremony took place on July 31, 2026, at Borcea Air Base, also known as Fetești Air Base.
Spain has deployed seven EF-18M Hornet fighter jets to Romania. The deployment also includes three NH-90 helicopters tasked with counter-drone operations and one A400M tanker aircraft for aerial refueling.
This is the fourth deployment of Spanish forces to Romania. Previous deployments took place in 2021, 2024, and February 2026.
The deployment is part of Spain’s national “Persistent Effort” operation and is expected to continue until December 2026.
The mission is formally classified not as traditional Air Policing, but as part of NATO’s broader Air Defence concept within the Integrated Air and Missile Defence (IAMD) system.

articles.title: Iran’s accusing Qatar of holding Iranian pilots an attempt to ‘flip narrative,’ analyst to 'Post'
articles.body:
Iran’s accusations that Qatar is holding three Iranian pilots shot down during attacks on Gulf states are an attempt to “flip the narrative” on Tehran’s “failed military gamble,” Gulf analysts told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff wrote in a letter published by the IRGC-affiliated Fars News Agency on Saturday that it had appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross to help secure the release of three Iranian pilots it claims have been held by Qatar since a failed mission to attack US military bases in March.
Qatar denied holding the Iranian pilots. The Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesperson confirmed on X that search-and-rescue teams had found the remains of one of the pilots and that Doha had contacted Iran to coordinate their handover. The spokesperson also said Tehran had yet to respond to an invitation to review details of Qatar’s search-and-rescue operations.
Dr. Ahmed Alkhuzaie, a Bahraini political analyst and managing partner at Khuzaie Associates LLC, told the Post that he believed Iran had deliberately chosen to make the accusation at this point to “flip the narrative after a failed military gamble.”
Alkhuzaie said Iran’s decision to drag a “neutral Gulf state,” which has largely acted as an ally for Tehran, into its war with the United States was a clear miscalculation, and that Doha had reacted “as any sovereign nation would” to the attacks.
“Its air defenses downed two Iranian Su-24s that violated its airspace. This was not aggression; it was self-defense,” he insisted. “The facts are clear: jets were shot down, one pilot’s remains were recovered, and no evidence supports Iran’s claim of captured servicemen.”
By depicting Qatar as having disappeared its pilots, Alkhuzaie said Tehran was attempting to “recast itself as the victim” to stir sympathy, pressure Doha and “distract from the reality that its plans failed.”
“This is political theater, not truth,” he said, adding that this reframing was part of Iran’s broader pattern. When its attacks succeed, they are depicted as a sign of the Islamic Republic’s strength, while when it loses, it “reframes the outcome to claim victimhood.”
Iran seeks to recast failed strategy as victimhood
“In the end, the narrative is simple. Iran struck Qatar, Qatar defended itself, and Iran is now trying to rewrite the story. The world should see this for what it is: a failed strategy dressed up as victimhood,” he said.
Mohammad Baqerzadeh, commander of the Committee for the Search for Missing Persons of Iran’s Armed Forces General Staff, also accused Kuwait of withholding information about the fate of four Iranians held in the country.
Iran admitted in May that the four Iranians, who were affiliated with the Revolutionary Guards, had entered Kuwaiti waters, claiming that the incident was caused by a navigational disruption. Kuwait said the four were suspected of planning hostile actions against the country and arrested them.
Qatar’s ‘complete transparency’ on issue works in its favor
Qatar’s complete “transparency” on the issue has worked in its favor, Alkhuzaie said. Doha invited Iranian officials to review its search operations in April, an offer that was “declined” by Tehran, he said, adding that Tehran’s refusal to accept Qatar’s invitation undermined its own claims.
The stakes for Doha are also too high for it to risk secretly holding Iranian pilots, he argued. Its position as a mediator would be threatened, as would its reputation and credibility in the Gulf.
Alkhuzaie said the issue was “less about facts than about credibility.” Iran has not provided evidence to support its accusations, offering little more than the pilots’ names, and has no reason to believe the men are alive, he said, making “the accusation look like propaganda timed to distract from a failed strike on al-Udeid Air Base.”

articles.title: Trump's envoys in Middle East to push for Gaza peace plan
articles.body:
Trump's envoys in Middle East to push for Gaza peace plan
CAIRO, Aug 16 - Donald Trump's envoys meet with Egyptian, Qatari and Turkish mediators in Cairo on Sunday, a diplomatic source said, in a bid to advance the U.S. president's Gaza peace plan, even as Israel pressed on with airstrikes in the enclave.
Hamas officials were present at some of the meetings between mediators and with Trump's envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, and Nickolay Mladenov, Trump's Board of Peace envoy for Gaza, the diplomat said.
A senior Israeli official said that Kushner and Mladenov were scheduled to meet on Monday with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who on August 9 said Trump's latest roadmap for Gaza peace was 'unacceptable'.
GAZA MEDICS SAY STRIKES INJURED SEVERAL PEOPLE
The official said that Israel was concerned about Washington's demand to end targeted assassinations of Hamas militants in Gaza as the group rebuilds its forces.
Trump's peace plan calls for the immediate cessation of military operations in Gaza. It foresees Hamas disarming as Israeli troops withdraw from the enclave and Gaza is rebuilt under a new civilian Palestinian administration.
After scaling back its attacks in the enclave earlier this month, Israel's airstrikes have resumed in the past few days.
The Israeli military said on Sunday that its aircraft targeted a militant in Khan Younis, in southern Gaza. At least five Palestinians were injured in the strike which had hit a tent encampment, medics in the enclave said.
A separate airstrike, which the Israeli military said targeted another militant, hit an apartment in the Nuseirat camp in central Gaza, wounding several people, medics said.
Earlier, Hamas leader Khalil Al-Hayya met with Egypt's intelligence chief Hassan Rashad in Cairo. Hamas spokesperson in Gaza, Hazem Qassem, said Al-Hayya would brief mediators on what he said were Israel's ceasefire violations.
Kushner had earlier met with Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi, Sisi's office said.
Trump announced last month that there had been a breakthrough in his plan to end the war, to which both Israel and Hamas had agreed.
Hamas said it had agreed to the plan to avoid a resumption of the war, but added that implementation of the deal would depend on Israel first meeting its own commitments, including withdrawing its forces and halting attacks.
An October ceasefire halted major fighting in a devastating two-year war in Gaza that was sparked by Hamas' October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, but it failed to end Israeli attacks entirely.
Israeli fire has killed more than 1,250 Palestinians in Gaza, most of them civilians, since October. It is unclear how many of those killed were militants, as Hamas does not usually disclose information about dead fighters.
Four Israeli soldiers were killed by militants in Gaza over the same period, according to Israeli figures. REUTERS

Iran accuses Qatar of thwarting probe into fate of its pilots

- Qatar denies holding the pilots, saying it invited Iran for briefings on rescue efforts but that Tehran did not respond.
- The incident ties into a wider Middle East conflict involving US and Israeli attacks on Iran, with ongoing tensions and failed peace talks.

TEHRAN – Iran accused Qatar on Aug 16 of thwarting efforts to work out what happened to three pilots Tehran says were captured during the Middle East war, though the Gulf state has denied detaining them.
Iran previously reported that one pilot was killed and others missing after a sortie to Qatar in March, but did not claim at the time that any of them was captured.
“A team of experts from the Iranian Air Force has been waiting for several months to travel to Qatar to conduct an on-site investigation,” said Iranian general Mohammad Bagherzadeh.
“However, due to persistent delays by Qatari authorities, the return of our brave pilots to their homeland remains impossible,” he added, according to the Tasnim news agency.
He called on Doha to authorise the team to travel to Qatar.
Bagherzadeh accused Qatar on Aug 15 of having captured three Iranian pilots who were carrying out an operation against the United States’ Al Udeid air base in early March and demanded their release.
Qatar denied holding the pilots and said an invitation was sent to Iran “to be briefed on the details of the search & rescue operations in April, but the Iranian side has yet to respond”.
Iran’s military said in July it retrieved the body of pilot Majid Kazemi, who was killed during the attack on Al Udeid.
The largest US military base in the Middle East, Al Udeid hosts forward elements of US Central Command, as well as its air and special operations forces.
In early March, Qatar’s Defence Ministry said it shot down two Iranian Sukhoi Su-24 bombers.
It was not immediately clear whether they were the same aircraft referred to by Iran, as Qatar and other countries across the region faced retaliatory attacks following the US and Israeli strikes that triggered the war.
It was the first time a Gulf country reported shooting down Iranian aircraft since the war broke out on Feb 28.
Diplomatic efforts led to an April ceasefire that ended nearly 40 days of fighting, followed by the signing of a framework for peace talks in June that later collapsed.
Iran and the US have since traded fire sporadically, with fighting mainly centred in southern Iran and around the Strait of Hormuz.

articles.title: Spanish F-18 shoots down suspected Russian drone over Romania
articles.body:
Necva Tastan Sevinc
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
Spanish F-18 fighter jets deployed on a NATO air defense mission shot down a suspected Russian drone after it entered Romanian airspace early Sunday, authorities said.
Romania’s Defense Ministry said its surveillance systems detected the aerial target at 4.44 am local time (0144GMT), approximately 24 kilometers (15 miles) north of the southeastern city of Galati, according to Romanian broadcaster Antena 3 CNN.
The drone entered Romanian airspace from the direction of neighboring Moldova, the ministry said.
Two Spanish F-18 fighter jets, which had been deployed preventively from the Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base, were authorized to intervene after establishing radar contact with the target.
The drone was shot down at 5.01 am (0201GMT) over an unpopulated area, with the operation coordinated through NATO’s Combined Air Operations Center in Torrejon, Spain.
Authorities identified a possible debris impact site between the localities of Baleni and Cudalbi in Galati County. Helicopters were dispatched as part of a search operation for the wreckage.
No casualties or property damage were immediately reported.
NATO’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe said the origin of the drone remained under investigation but that it appeared to be Russian.
“Further details of Sunday’s incident remain under investigation, but the drone appears to be Russian,” spokesperson Col. Martin O’Donnell said.
Romania’s acting Foreign Minister Oana Toiu said allies had been informed about the incident.
“Romania is on the front line of NATO and European Union border defense. We have informed our allies and will continue to build a strong defense and deterrent force on the eastern flank,” she said on US social media platform X.
Toiu said it was the third drone to illegally enter Romanian airspace and be shot down in the past three weeks.
Romania's presidential adviser, Marius Lazurca, thanked Spain for its role in the operation, saying: “Our full gratitude to Spain for participating in NATO Air Policing!”
Romania shares a 614-kilometer (382-mile) border with Ukraine and has experienced repeated airspace violations during Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports along the Danube River.

articles.title: Ukrainian rapper mocked Russia’s claim he helped deliver drones for attacks near Moscow. A month later, Russia allegedly tried to kill him in Poland
articles.body:
On 14 August 2026, Polish broadcaster RMF FM identified American-Ukrainian rapper and video blogger Kyivstoner as the previously unnamed target of an alleged Russian-directed assassination plot in Warsaw. The case comes as European authorities investigate suspected Russian attacks and sabotage across the continent.
The alleged plot against Kyivstoner comes amid attacks on Kremlin critics abroad, including the fatal shooting of a Russian opposition artist in Poland in June.
Polish authorities disclosed the Kyivstoner's case on 13 August but withheld the target’s identity. RMF’s identification points to a possible motive, though it relies on unverified allegations from the FSB, Russia's domestic security agency that Kyivstoner of managed drone deliveries intended for attacks near Moscow.
Who is Kyivstoner?
Kyivstoner was born Albert Vasiliev and uses the name Slevin Dadyan on his US passport. He gained attention through humorous videos and the Ukrainian group Hryby before releasing solo tracks, including “Leto” (Summer) and “Zvuk” (Sound).
In a 2025 interview, Vasiliev voiced support for Ukrainians and opposition to Russian occupation, saying Russian ruler Vladimir Putin made him angry and that he wanted civilians and soldiers to stop dying.
In July 2026, Russia’s FSB accused Kyivstoner of overseeing logistics for a foiled drone attack on a defense enterprise near Moscow.
The agency alleged that 35 drones assembled in Kyiv were concealed in a shipment of ceramic tiles and smuggled into Russia through Slovakia, Poland, and Belarus. Russian authorities also added Vasiliev to a register of people they label as involved in extremist or terrorist activity.
Vasiliev responded on Instagram by mocking Russia's allegation, saying he had been relaxing and playing video games rather than organizing an attack.
Russian authorities also accuse him of cooperating with Ukrainian intelligence. He denies the accusations, and RMF offered no independent evidence to substantiate them.
Suspect detained before alleged attack
Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Polish services detained the Russian suspect on 7 August, stopping the alleged attack “at the last minute.” US services assisted the operation. A Polish court remanded the man in custody for three months.
The journalists described the Russian citizen as a native of Donbas in eastern Ukraine. Tusk said the target, who holds Ukrainian and US passports, was “inconvenient to the Putin regime.”
The prime minister called it the first Russian-ordered attempt of its kind against a US citizen in another NATO country.
Killings and disrupted plots across Europe
Throughout Europe, Russia has tried to hunt down and kill anti-Kremlin critics and supporters of Ukraine. In June, Russian opposition artist Robert Kuzovkov, known as Semyon Skrepetsky, was shot dead in eastern Poland. Hours earlier, he had reported threats from “Russian patriots.” Polish authorities detained two Belarusian nationals, but have not attributed the killing to Moscow.
US and German services also reportedly foiled a Russian plot against Rheinmetall CEO Armin Papperger in 2024. German intelligence later treated the surveillance of Bavarian drone manufacturer Donaustahl’s CEO as a suspected planned assassination.

Ukraine Snaps Russia’s “Arrow,” Hitting Strela-10 Air Defense, Drone Depot and Command Posts
Ukrainian forces struck a Russian air defense system, military storage facilities, and two command posts across temporarily occupied parts of the Donetsk, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions, Ukraine’s General Staff reported on August 15.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The strikes were carried out throughout August 14 and overnight into August 15 against facilities used by Russian forces for air defense, logistics, drone operations, and battlefield command.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces struck a Russian Strela-10 short-range surface-to-air missile system in temporarily occupied Kreminna, Luhansk region.
The Strela-10 is a Soviet-designed mobile air defense system mounted on a tracked armored vehicle and designed to protect ground forces from low-flying aircraft, helicopters, and other aerial targets at short ranges.
A Russian drone storage facility in temporarily occupied Vuhledar, Donetsk region, was also hit. In temporarily occupied Lysychansk, Luhansk region, Ukrainian forces targeted a depot containing logistical and material supplies used by Russian troops.
Two Russian command posts were among the other targets. The General Staff identified their locations as temporarily occupied Selydove in the Donetsk region and temporarily occupied Mykhailivka in the Zaporizhzhia region.
Ukraine’s General Staff said the extent of the damage and the final results of the strikes were still being assessed.
The strikes came as Ukrainian forces continued operations against Russian military and defense-industrial facilities both in temporarily occupied Ukrainian territories and inside Russia.
On August 15, Ukrainian forces also struck the Progress Rocket Space Centre in Samara and the Savasleyka military airfield in Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region. articles.title: The Times: Ukraine Used British Nyan Drones to Attack Oil Refineries
articles.body:
Ukraine used British-made Nyan attack drones to strike Russian oil refineries in Volgograd and Yaroslavl.
The Times reported the attacks.
The Nyan drone was developed by British company Callen-Lenz, which is part of FalconWorks, the technology division of BAE Systems.
The drone has a wingspan of 2.9 meters and a maximum takeoff weight of more than 75 kg. It is launched using a pneumatic catapult.
The aircraft is powered by a single gas turbine engine. It has a cruising speed of 120 knots, or about 222 km/h, and a reported range of more than 250 km.
The drone can carry up to 20 kg of payload. Its modular design allows different equipment to be installed depending on the mission.
Nyan drones have been in service with the Ukrainian Defense Forces for some time.
In late June 2024, an identical drone was found on Russian territory. At the time, it was mistakenly identified as a new Ukrainian kamikaze drone.
It later emerged that the drone is manufactured by British company Callen-Lenz at a facility in Wiltshire. In addition to Ukraine, Nyan drones have also entered service with the British Army.
The first unit to receive these drones was the 26th Regiment Royal Artillery, part of the 3rd Division. The British military uses Nyan as a long-range strike system and to complement the artillery capabilities of its units.
The drone was initially tested in Estonia during the annual Spring Storm exercises, where the Royal Artillery conducted test launches and practiced coordination. Following the trials, the regiment officially adopted the Nyan UAV into service.
Its use is expected to expand to other units in the future.
To expand the drone’s operational capabilities, the British Army, together with the Royal Navy, also tested launching it from a surface vessel.
In June 2026, a catapult was installed on the experimental vessel XV Patrick Blackett, from which a Nyan drone was launched.
Back in February 2026, Callen-Lenz was awarded a £4.99 million contract (approximately $6.7 million) by the UK Ministry of Defence to supply Nyan OWE systems to enhance deep-strike capabilities.
According to the official explanation, Nyan became the only mass-produced system of its class registered in the Military Aircraft Register. This was a key factor in selecting the system for rapid deployment.

articles.title: Houthis launch new attacks in Mocha, Marib amid mounting escalation in Yemen
articles.body:
Mohammed Sameai and Serdar Dincel
16 August 2026•Update: 16 August 2026
The Houthi group launched a new wave of drone and missile attacks in Mocha and Marib in southwestern Yemen as escalation continues to rise in the war-torn Arab country, according to pro-government forces and local media on Sunday.
The National Resistance Forces, aligned with Yemen’s internationally recognized government and led by Presidential Leadership Council member Tariq Saleh, said one missile hit Mocha, without giving details about injuries or damage.
In Marib, the provincial government’s media office said six ballistic missiles and four drones targeted residential neighborhoods in the city Saturday evening, injuring four people and causing damage to homes and civilian property.
A statement by the media office said one strike hit a bakery in the Al-Sharika neighborhood north of Marib city, wounding one person.
Strikes also targeted several neighborhoods in the densely populated city, damaging vehicles and homes, the statement said.
The media office called on the international community to “condemn these attacks and crimes targeting displacement camps, residential neighborhoods and civilian facilities, and document them as violations of international humanitarian law.”
The Houthis have not yet commented on the report.
Mocha and Marib have come under repeated Houthi attacks in recent days amid mounting escalation across the war-torn country.
Yemen has witnessed a relative lull since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Fighting has resumed in several provinces in recent weeks, including Marib, Al-Jawf, Al-Dhalea and Taiz, as the country continues to face one of the world’s worst humanitarian and economic crises.

articles.title: “One of the most massive” Ukrainian drone attacks hits Moscow Oblast: two major warehouses ablaze
articles.body:
A drone hit a major Wildberries warehouse at Koledino near Moscow overnight on 16 August 2026 and set it ablaze, Moscow Oblast Governor Andrey Vorobyov said. Vorobyov described the overnight swarm as “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent times.”
It comes amid an expanding Ukrainian campaign against Wildberries, Russia's largest online retailer with a vast network of warehouses and logistics centers, that has reached warehouses from Moscow Oblast to the Urals. Ukrainian authorities say Wildberries facilities are used to supply components for Russian drone production and navigation equipment, making them part of Russia’s wartime logistics network.
The Koledino fire puts a major part of Wildberries’ storage and sorting capacity at risk. At about 250,000 square meters, the complex is one of the retailer’s largest logistics hubs. Ukrainian sources say the marketplace has moved drone parts and other military-linked goods. Wildberries denies supporting Russia’s military.
Wildberries’ parent company, RWB, confirmed the fire, saying workers had been evacuated and deliveries rerouted.
Unlike the 28 July fire at Koledino industrial park, the latest blaze was confirmed at Wildberries’ own Koledino warehouse. Initial reports in July had also pointed to Wildberries, but open-source investigators later identified the burning building as a neighboring warehouse run by a third-party logistics company.
A second fire broke out at Warehouse No. 15 in MLP Severnoye Domodedovo, a multimodal logistics complex near one of Moscow’s main airports. Vorobyov said the warehouse stores medications.
Vorobyov claimed an 83-year-old man was killed after a drone fell on a private home in the Ramenskoye district, while at least six other people were injured across the region.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin claimed that Russian air defenses destroyed 201 drones approaching the region.
Ukraine confirms Wildberries warehouse was targeted
Ukraine’s Defense Ministry confirmed that the Wildberries logistics hub in the Koledino industrial park was put out of operation during the overnight drone attack.
The ministry said the facility, which covered 250,000 square meters, was Wildberries’ largest warehouse by area. It also said Ukraine has now disabled seven of the company’s 10 largest logistics centers.
Ukraine’s campaign against Wildberries keeps growing
Ukraine’s campaign against Wildberries began on 18 July 2026, when drones struck warehouses in Elektrostal and Kotovsk. Reported attacks have since reached the retailer’s sites across Russia, including a newly opened hub near Voronezh and a warehouse in Tver targeted three times in two weeks.
By 14 August, Agentstvo had counted fires at more than 20 Wildberries sites. The sustained attacks had already prompted Wildberries to prohibit warehouse workers from bringing smartphones to work, citing concerns that photos and videos taken during drone alerts could pose a security risk.
The effects on Russia’s economy
The number and geographic spread of Ukraine’s strikes have put sustained pressure on the retailer’s nationwide warehouse network and Russia’s economy at large.
Earlier fires destroyed goods belonging to independent sellers, The Moscow Times reported. Wildberries said it was considering compensation, although its contracts do not require the company to cover losses caused by drone attacks.
In response to Ukraine’s strikes, the company has also reportedly sought additional storage in Kazakhstan, giving local warehouse operators greater leverage as it tries to replace capacity lost in Russia.
The physical disruption was followed on 15 August by a Ukrainian cyberattack targeting Wildberries’ payment and customer service systems. The hackers said customers could not make payments or reach the company through its main online support channel.

The signatories called for at least 24 hours’ advance notice of tests and other launches of intercontinental ballistic missiles, submarine-launched missiles and space launch vehicles.
The proposal also calls for notifying other countries of the missile class, launch area, flight direction and danger zones for sailors and pilots.
On August 11, China launched a space launch vehicle, but it exploded shortly after liftoff. Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung condemned Beijing’s actions.

According to preliminary Japanese estimates, the missile traveled about 690 km and reached a maximum altitude of approximately 90 km. It fell into the Sea of Japan outside Japan’s exclusive economic zone.
Lin Chia-lung said Beijing is attempting to unilaterally change the status quo in the Taiwan Strait and the Indo-Pacific region through military pressure, economic coercion and “gray-zone” tactics.

articles.title: Ukraine Sends Record 600 Drones Toward Moscow Region
articles.body:
According to the mayor of Moscow, 600 Ukrainian drones were detected over a 24-hour period “in the direction of the Moscow region.” This is the largest number of Ukrainian strike drones to have headed toward the Russian capital since the beginning of the war.
Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin reported the drone attack on his Telegram channel.
During the attack, Ukraine’s Defense Forces struck Wildberries warehouses in Koledino and the Severnoye Domodedovo logistics facility near Moscow.
This suggests that the intensity of Ukraine’s long-range strikes continues to increase in August. During July, 6,225 drones were launched toward Moscow and the Moscow region, while in just the first 16 days of August, at least 4,327 UAVs were launched toward the Moscow region.
The average daily number of drones targeting Moscow and neighboring regions increased from approximately 201 in July to 290 in the first half of August, an increase of nearly 44%.
The figures are part of a broader trend of intensifying Ukrainian strikes. OSINT analysts from the Oko Gora channel recorded 65 confirmed strikes by Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles in July, 55% more than in June.
The targets included 17 oil refineries, 16 logistics centers, 10 oil depots, nine ports, four defense industry enterprises, three vessels and two airfields.
These figures do not include the campaign of strikes against vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea or attacks on temporarily occupied territories.
For comparison, during the first 15 days of August, analysts from ExileNova+ had already recorded at least 43 facilities struck by long-range drones and missiles.
These included 22 logistics infrastructure facilities, as well as oil refineries and military airfields. Compared with July, the average daily rate of confirmed strikes increased by approximately 37%.
Ukraine first surpassed Russia in the number of long-range drones launched in March 2026 and has maintained this lead consistently since May. At the same time, Russian forces have begun shifting their focus to the use of large numbers of jet-powered drones, which are more difficult to counter with interceptor drones.
On August 15, Flamingo cruise missiles struck an industrial site in Samara that houses the Aviakor and Progress Rocket Space Centre enterprises. The latter produces Soyuz-2 launch vehicles.
According to the Varta OSINT project, Progress is one of the key enterprises in Russia’s rocket and space industry. The company develops and produces launch vehicles, including the Soyuz-2 family, which are used to launch Russia’s equivalent of Starlink, the Rassvet communications satellites.

Russia Builds Up Jet-Powered Drone Strike Hub Near Ukraine. Here’s What Satellite Images Reveal
Russian forces have completed the deployment of 16 launchers for jet-powered attack drones at the Tsymbulova drone base in Russia’s Oryol region, while satellite imagery also shows more than 100 drones stored in the open at the facility.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to satellite imagery published by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Strategic Aviation on August 15, the new infrastructure includes 10 launchers designed for Geran-5 drones and six for Geran-4 UAVs. The work was completed over roughly one month.
The facility also contains four launchers for Geran-3 drones and three launchers for the more widely used Geran-2, the Russian designation for Shahed-type attack drones.
Satellite images reviewed by Strategic Aviation show at least 37 Geran-5 and eight Geran-4 jet-powered drones positioned at the site, alongside 56 Geran-2 attack UAVs.
The imagery also indicates that Russia is expanding storage capacity at Tsymbulova. Construction is continuing in the western section of the base, where smaller drone storage buildings are being added alongside larger warehouse facilities.
Russia has additionally installed nearly 100 solar panels across the site. According to Strategic Aviation, they are intended to provide supplementary power for communications equipment, weather stations, and drone guidance systems, increasing the facility’s ability to continue operating during possible power disruptions.
The Tsymbulova drone base is located near the village of Tsymbulova in Russia’s Oryol region, approximately 175–180 kilometers from the Ukrainian border.
The expansion comes as Russia increases production of its newer jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 12 that Russian manufacturers are producing approximately 3,000 Geran-4 and Geran-5 drones per month, with serial production established at the Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan.

articles.title: Ukrainian drone attack kills civilian in Moscow Region – governor
articles.body:
Ukrainian drone attack kills civilian in Moscow Region – governor
An 83-year-old man died and six more people were injured as a result of an overnight Ukrainian drone strike in Moscow Region, local governor Andrey Vorobyev has said, adding that electronic warfare shot down or intercepted 187 Ukrainian UAVs.
The strike comes as Kiev has intensified long-range attacks on Russian civilian infrastructure and residential areas. Earlier this month, a Ukrainian drone struck a crowded beach in the southern resort of Gelendzhik, killing at least seven people, including three children, and injuring dozens more.
Drones were intercepted over Domodedovo, Podolsk, Stupino, Odintsovo, Naro-Fominsk, Ramenskoye, Chekhov, Kolomna, Kashira, and Yegoryevsk, Vorobyev said on Sunday in a post on Telegram.
The governor said that the 83-year-old man was killed when a drone fell on the grounds of a private house. Three people were injured in Podolsk as a truck driver suffered a hand injury in Klimovsk. Another man sustained shrapnel wounds at the Lesnoy allotment association, where a private house was also damaged, while a woman in the settlement of Zheleznodorozhny suffered a shoulder injury. None of the injuries were life-threatening, Vorobyev added.
Several homes and a shopping center were damaged in Domodedovo, where a balcony also caught fire. A private house and a church school were damaged in Chekhov, while a bathhouse was destroyed in Stupino, Vorobyev noted.
A storage facility linked to e-commerce giant Wildberries caught fire after a drone strike in the Koledino industrial park in Podolsk, while a warehouse storing medicines caught fire in Domodedovo. Damage was also reported at a newly built police department in Kashira and at industrial facilities in Voskresensk. A power line was damaged in the Matveyevskoye cottage settlement, the governor specified.
Wildberries press office confirmed the fire at its warehouse in Podolsk, saying that the facility had been evacuated and deliveries rerouted to other sites.
Russia’s Defense Ministry reported on Sunday that 822 Ukrainian drones were destroyed over Russian regions and the Black and Azov seas. Five people were killed in the Rostov Region, while attacks also injured civilians in Belgorod and Bryansk regions. Damage was reported in several regions, including to homes, public buildings, and industrial facilities. In Belgorod, a drone attack on a civilian bus killed one woman and injured nine more people.
Russian authorities have condemned Kiev’s drone raids as terrorist attacks targeting civilians. In May, a triple wave of Ukrainian UAV strikes on a student dormitory in Donbass’ Starobelsk killed 21 people, mostly teenage girls, and partially collapsed the five-storey building.
Russia has responded to the raids by stepping up its long-range missile and drone strikes on Ukraine’s military-industrial and logistical infrastructure. Moscow maintains that it never targets civilians, only military sites and infrastructure supporting Kiev’s forces.

articles.title: NATO fighter jet shoots down drone over Romania
articles.body:
A Spanish F-18 fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission Sunday shot down a drone that had illegally entered Romanian airspace.
The drone was detected by radar about 24 kilometers north of the eastern city of Galați after entering Romania from Moldova. Having established radar contact, the fighter jet was authorized to shoot it down at 5:01 a.m. Authorities said debris from the destroyed aircraft had fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages.
Martin O'Donnell, spokesperson for NATO operation headquarters, said additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remained under investigation but that the drone "appears to be Russian.”

"The Ministry of National Defence is constantly monitoring the situation and informs in real time the allied structures about such events," the ministry added in a statement.
It is the fourth drone shot down by NATO over Romania since the beginning of 2026. In July, Romanian F-16s downed three Russian drones that breached the country's airspace — the first such interceptions after dozens of incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați, injuring two people.
Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine traded strikes over the weekend. Russian forces launched missile and drone attacks on Kyiv early Sunday, sparking fires in at least two districts and injuring three people, according to the city's military administration.
Ukrainian drones also struck the Moscow region overnight in what the regional governor Andrei Vorobyov described as one of the largest attacks to target the area, killing an 83-year-old man.

articles.title: Ukraine Tests Last Shadow T200 Interceptor Drone, Exceeding Expected Range
articles.body:
Ukraine has tested a new interceptor drone capable of flying more than 120 kilometers (74 miles) as Kyiv seeks cheaper ways to destroy Russian unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) targeting its cities and front lines.
The ‘Last Shadow T200’ reached 122 kilometers (76 miles) during recent combat trials, well beyond the 70-kilometer (43-mile) range originally expected, developer Ukrainska Bavovna told Ukrainian defense news outlet Militarnyi.

The aircraft maintained a stable video link throughout the test, according to the company, potentially expanding the distance over which Ukrainian forces can operate the interceptor.
The T200 is designed to defend cities and operate along the frontline against targets including Shahed and Geran attack drones, Gerbera decoys and Molniya drones, company representatives told Militarnyi.
It has a stated top speed of 300 kilometers (186 miles) per hour, can operate at altitudes of up to 16,400 feet (4,999 meters) and can remain airborne for about an hour at cruising speed.
Ukrainska Bavovna began developing the interceptor last year, and both the airframe and its warhead have been approved for use by Ukraine’s defense ministry.
Anti-spoofing defense
The aircraft is equipped with a movable camera designed to improve target detection.
Its video system can also switch between channels and frequency bands to counter Shtora, a Russian system designed to disrupt or spoof drone video feeds.

Quote: "The enemy struck Kryvyi Rih. Industrial facilities were targeted. A fire broke out. Rescue workers are working at the scene."
Details: At 04:25, Hanzha reported that one person had been killed and six others had been injured in the attack.
According to satellite data from NASA's FIRMS fire and thermal anomaly monitoring service, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine's largest mining and metallurgical company, may have been hit.
Later, ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih confirmed that the company had been hit.
Update: In the morning, Hanzha said that the number of people injured had risen to 13.
Quote: "A 48-year-old man has been taken to hospital in a serious condition. Ten people have been taken to hospital in a moderate condition. The other injured people are undergoing examinations."
Update: After 10:00, Dnipropetrovsk Oblast Military Administration said that rescue workers had recovered another body from under the rubble.
Fourteen more people sustained injuries; of them, 11 were taken to hospital, and a 48-year-old man is in a serious condition.
Background:
- On the night of 15-16 August, Russian forces launched a large-scale attack on several regions of Ukraine using ballistic missiles and attack drones, targeting Kyiv, Kryvyi Rih, Kamianske and Kremenchuk.
- Oleksandr Vilkul, Head of the Kryvyi Rih Defence Council, had reported that the city was under a combined attack involving ballistic missiles and UAVs.

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 11 Chinese military aircraft and 10 ships
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked 11 Chinese military aircraft, eight naval vessels, and two official ships between 6 a.m. on Saturday and the same time Sunday.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems. Seven of the People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern and central air defense identification zones, or ADIZ, according to the ministry.
So far this month, Taiwan has tracked Chinese military aircraft 126 times and ships 189 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around Taiwan.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Hamas, Hezbollah coordinating attacks with Iran as IDF warns of rebuilt ‘axis of evil’
articles.body:
Hamas and Hezbollah have begun coordinating their increased activity with Iranian assistance in recent weeks, the IDF has assessed, as the military has identified increased friction between Israeli forces and terrorists on both the northern and southern fronts.
The IDF has expressed that the coordination is likely an effort to rebuild its axis of evil that would increase pressure on Israel.
According to a military source, a ‘battle of wits’ is taking place around the Ali Taher ridge between the Northern Command and Hezbollah.
The terrorist organization is trying to determine where IDF troops are positioned, and when it detects movement, it attempts to attack in a "gray area," as it did early Saturday morning with a fiber-optic drone. Three soldiers from the IDF's Yahalom special engineering unit, operating under the Commando Brigade combat team, were wounded as a result.
Hezbollah attempts to resupply operatives trapped underground
At the same time, according to reports, Hezbollah is attempting to resupply its operatives who are trapped in underground infrastructure. The IDF, meanwhile, is trying to locate Hezbollah infrastructure and terrorists on the Ali Taher ridge and destroy them.
"Whoever comes out of the underground and surrenders will be taken for questioning in Israel, and whoever remains underground will either die, or we will kill him," a senior military source said.
The Northern Command is also conducting a complex intelligence effort to locate all hidden supply routes and drone activity intended to resupply Hezbollah operatives in the area.
"We are blocking access to the area where they are located. They will not be able to hold out forever," a senior military source familiar with the details said.
According to reports, the operatives have been emerging from underground to search for food.
"What happened on Saturday was that they exposed us with a drone. Whoever is more determined will win. A lot of patience is needed," the source added.
In response, the IDF struck in the Nabatieh area and within territory under the IDF's operational control. Beirut and senior officials from the Shi'ite organization who are hiding there have remained off-limits due to a US demand.
IDF tank drives over explosive device in Gaza Strip
Meanwhile, an IDF tank drove over an explosive device in the southern Gaza Strip. According to IDF assessments, the device was planted recently.
Although the Southern Command views the incident as an escalation in the friction along the Yellow Line, the political leadership did not authorize a broad strike in the heart of Gaza City, again due to sensitivities with the White House, which is demanding an immediate halt to strikes in Gaza City and targeted killings, except in cases involving the removal of an immediate threat.

articles.title: Houthis launch new attacks on al-Makha and Marib as Yemen conflict escalates
articles.body:
Houthis launch new attacks on al-Makha and Marib as Yemen conflict escalates
The Houthis launched a wave of missiles and drones at Yemen’s Marib city and the coastal city of al-Makha (Mocha) overnight, killing several people, according to local media reports.
An attack on Sunday hit the outskirts of al-Makha, a port city on Yemen’s Red Sea coast, while another struck a main road in the city.

Four people were killed and eight were injured in the overnight attacks, according to state media and the director of the al-Makha airport.
Marib’s government media office said six ballistic missiles and four drones targeted residential neighbourhoods in the city on Saturday evening, wounding four people and causing damage to homes and civilian infrastructure.
Port operations in al-Makha were already paused due to several days of strikes, Abdulmalik al-Sharabi, the director general of the government-controlled facility, said on Saturday.
Meanwhile, the Yemeni military said it launched 181 operations against Houthi positions in several governorates on Saturday and Sunday, killing and wounding dozens of members of the group.
The Houthis said four members were killed, but did not provide further details on the circumstances of their deaths.
Yemen had witnessed a relative lull in fighting since April 2022 in a war that began nearly 12 years ago between government forces and the Houthis, who have controlled the capital, Sanaa, and other cities and provinces since September 2014.
Earlier this month, the Houthis launched strikes on military camps in Marib and Hadramout, killing at least 30 government soldiers, in the deadliest single episode of the conflict in years. Fighting has since resumed in several provinces, including al-Jawf, al-Dhalea and Taiz.

articles.title: Ukraine hit the plant that fuels Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S rockets Russia fires at frontline cities with no metro to shelter in
articles.body:
Ukraine struck the plant that fuels the rockets Russia rains on its frontline cities. On the night of 16 August 2026, Ukraine's Defense Forces hit an important Russian military-industrial enterprise, the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, Rostov Oblast, and a fire was recorded at the site, the General Staff reported.
The plant makes the fuel for weapons that Russia uses to grind down Ukrainian civilian areas. The Kamensky Combine produces solid rocket fuel for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems, which Russia fires at frontline cities like Zaporizhzhia, where there is no metro to shelter in and civilians have only minutes to get behind walls the rockets punch through easily.
The Tornado-S is one of Russia’s most advanced long-range rocket artillery systems, capable of striking targets up to 120 kilometers away. Russian “Tornado-S” and “Smerch” systems are designed to fire and retreat rapidly, making them extremely difficult to locate.
The target feeds Russia's rocket artillery
The Kamensky Combine is a node in Russia's weapons production. It produces solid rocket fuel for the rocket systems, as well as a range of missile systems and aviation strike weapons, with its output directly serving the needs of Russia's armed forces.
The damage is still being assessed. The extent of the damage and the results of the strike are being clarified, the General Staff said, with a fire confirmed at the site.
Two earlier strikes were confirmed hit
The General Staff also confirmed results from recent deep strikes. Analysis of additional data confirmed the shutdown of the ZapSibNeftekhim complex in Tobolsk, Tyumen Oblast, one of Russia's largest petrochemical plants, after its central gas-fractionation unit was struck on 10 August.
A refinery was confirmed to have been hit, too. The 11 August strike at the Orsknaftaorgsyntez refinery in Orsk, Orenburg Oblast, damaged its hydrocracking unit, several primary oil-processing units, and a secondary distillation unit. The refinery produces gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel, and other products for Russia's armed forces and military industry.
The campaign continues
The General Staff signaled more to come. Work on key military and military-industrial targets of the enemy continues, it said, closing with "to be continued."
That promise fits a campaign that has spent 2026 reaching ever deeper into Russia, hitting the refineries, petrochemical plants, and now rocket-fuel factories that supply the war. Each confirmed strike degrades a different piece of Russia's ability to produce the weapons and fuel its forces run on.

articles.title: Ukraine reports strike on Russian rocket fuel plant, petrochemical facility shuts down after earlier strikes
articles.body:
Ukraine reports strike on Russian rocket fuel plant, petrochemical facility shuts down after earlier strikes
Ukraine's defence forces struck the Kamensky Combine, a solid rocket fuel plant in Russia's Rostov Oblast, located near the Ukrainian border, on the night of 15-16 August. The General Staff has also reported on the effects of previous strikes on petrochemical plants in Tyumen Oblast, more than 2,000 km (1,240 miles) from the border, and Orenburg Oblast, approximately 1,500 km (930 miles) away.
Source: Ukraine's General Staff
Details: A fire was reported following the nighttime strike on the Kamensky Combine in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky.
The General Staff said the plant produces solid rocket fuel for the Uragan, Smerch, and Tornado-S multiple-launch rocket systems and other missile systems and airborne weapons.
The Ukrainian military also said that operations ceased at the Zapsibneftekhim plant in Tobolsk, Tyumen Oblast, one of Russia's largest petrochemical complexes, following the 10 August strike on Central Gas Fractionation Unit No. 1.
The General Staff also confirmed that several units at the Orsknefteorgsintez, a medium-sized oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia's Orenburg Oblast, had been hit on 11 August: a hydrocracking unit, three primary crude oil processing units and a secondary distillation unit for light petroleum fractions.
The refinery produces petrol, diesel, aviation fuel, fuel oil and other petroleum products used to supply Russian troops and the military-industrial complex, according to the General Staff.
Background: On the night of 15-16 August, Ukraine's defence forces struck a concentration area of a Russian missile unit in occupied Crimea, a railway bridge in Zaporizhzhia Oblast and military warehouses in Donetsk Oblast.

articles.title: Moscow strikes Ukrainian steel plant as Kyiv targets Russian economy
articles.body:
Moscow strikes Ukrainian steel plant as Kyiv targets Russian economy
Romania, which borders Ukraine, said an F-18 fighter on a Nato air policing mission had shot down a drone that breached its airspace during the latest attacks
Russia carried out a wave of air strikes on Ukraine overnight, killing two people at a steel plant, and Kyiv launched a heavy drone attack on the Moscow region that killed one person and set ablaze a warehouse used by Russia’s leading e-commerce retailer.
Romania, which borders Ukraine, said an F-18 fighter on a Nato air policing mission had shot down a drone that breached its airspace during the latest attacks. It did not specify the origin of the drone, which entered from Moldova, but a spokesperson for the treaty organisation said it appeared to be Russian.
Russia struck Ukraine’s largest grain export port on the River Danube near the Romanian border last week after stepping up attacks on Ukraine in recent weeks. Ukraine has also intensified attacks on Russian targets including oil refineries, and both sides have struck commercial vessels in the Black Sea.
In the latest attacks since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, Russian forces struck Ukraine’s biggest steel plant overnight in the industrial city of Kryvyi Rih, President Volodymyr Zelensky’s hometown.
At least two people were killed and 14 injured, Ukrainian officials said.
“As a result of the attack, key production facilities in the power generation and blast furnace sectors have been damaged, and the plant’s production processes have been partially halted,” steel manufacturer ArcelorMittal Kryvyi Rih said on social media.

articles.title: Young voices, visual poetics and new money shape Locarno 2026
articles.body:
Young voices, visual poetics and new money shape Locarno 2026
The 79th edition of the Locarno Film Festival combined coming-of-age tales with radical film poetics as record industry attendance pointed to a new wave of rising private investment in independent cinema.
Young audiences are returningExternal link to movie theatres, raising industry’s hopes that the massive impact of streaming services, video games and social media can be offset by a renewed appetite for shared cultural experiences.
Coincidence or not, a remarkable number of films at this year’s festival – many of which by debutante filmmakers – explore adolescence, coming-of-age experiences, and the social and political realities facing younger generations. Fittingly, Locarno’s top prize went to one of them.
Florin Șerban’s Romanian drama You Don’t Belong Here follows a widowed father unaware of the night-time activities of his teenage son who has joined a group of masked vigilantes.
The trend is seemingly global: from Argentina (The days Off, The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer) to Canada (Manhunt) and the United States (Destroy All Girls), to Ghana (Ego Reach We All) and Central African Republic (Congo Boy), as well as several European productions (the Swiss Portuguese Crocodile; the Italian Ketticè). From Ukraine, I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming adds gender themes to this mix, set against the backdrop of war.
Roughly half of the 32 films in Locarno’s two main competitions touch on youth, identity or coming of age. The subjects vary widely, but the pattern suggests a generation keen to see its experiences reflected on screen.
More
Florin Serban’s ‘You Don’t Belong Here’ wins Golden Leopard at Locarno
New ventures in town
The film industry appears to be paying attention. Media outlets tracking acquisitions and sales during the festival said attendance at Locarno Pro, the festival’s marketplace for producers, distributors and financiers, rose 10% from 2025 to a record of 2,140 accreditations – already building on what had been considered an all-time high the year before.
A closer look, however, revealed a new guest: venture capital. According to VarietyExternal link, private investors are discovering the value of the independent movie business despite its risks and unpredictable returns. “Shrinking broadcaster funding, international distributor investment and now state aid” are opening opportunities for private investors and forcing “the whole system to adapt to new players that will change the rules”, it wrote.
How that will reshape the sector remains unclear, especially for independent productions that don’t follow mainstream industry conventions. Rather than backing individual projects, investors are increasingly targeting the entire portfolios of well-established companies that include production, distribution and sales, such as Paris-based mk2, the online platform Mubi, or Red Bull Studios, the film arm of the energy drink conglomerate.
Lineup breakdown
Every year, critics debate the quality of Locarno’s official selection. While the section devoted to film classics, rarities, and critics’ choices is usually undisputed, the two main competitions – the Concorso Internazionale (international competition) and Cineasti del Presente, for authors’ first or second features – attract more debate.
Artistic director Giona A. Nazzaro assembled an eclectic main competition featuring both emerging filmmakers and established auteurs, such as Hong Sangsoo (South Korea), Nelson Yeo (Singapore), Gurvinder Singh (India) and Denis Côté (Canada). One of his boldest choices was to place Brazilian first-time directors Enock Carvalho and Matheus Farias (The Riverbank) in the main competition rather than Cineasti del Presente.
More
Brazil in Locarno: ‘The Riverbank’ sets Recife’s mangroves against the gospel of power
Nazzaro’s bet paid off: The Riverbank took the Special Jury Prize, reinforcing Locarno’s reputation as a platform for revealing new talent in Brazilian cinema, from Glauber Rocha to Kleber Mendonça Filho.
Cineasti del Presente pushed even further towards unconventional forms of storytelling. The Argentinian Alessandra Sanguinetti, worldwide renowned as a photographer, presented The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer, a documentary drawn from a more than 20-year photography project about two cousins as they grow up in the countryside of Buenos Aires.
The Brazilian Ana Vaz, who moves fluidly between fine arts and experimental film, presented Hanabi, also a project of over ten years in the making, about the Fukushima nuclear fallout (and planetary disaster).
A hybrid work blending cinema, literature and visual art, Hanabi can be easily categorized as ‘experimental’ – a label its creator Ana Vaz would firmly contest. “I don’t accept this inability of cinema to become anything other than what is defined by certain cinematic canons within the tradition of documentary cinema, essay cinema or fiction cinema,” she told Swissinfo.
Film poetics, real cinema
While Ana Vaz welcomes Nazzaro’s decision not to separate mainstream narratives from alternative, or so-called experimental, ones, she believes this puts such films at an unfair competitive disadvantage, as their chances to win prizes are considerably lower. Despite this Hanabi won a Special Mention prize.
For spectators, Sanguinetti’s and Vaz’s inclusion in the festival programme reinforced Locarno’s standing as a cinephile paradise. This year’s edition was especially rich with outstanding poetic works (due to the lack of a better word than ‘experimental’), starting with the homage to Swiss artist, graphic designer, photographer and filmmaker Isa Hesse-Rabinovitch (1917-2003), with the screening of two recently restored films, Siren Island (1981) and Ghosts and Guests (1989).
Hesse-Rabinovitch was recognised during her lifetime as a pioneer of feminist filmmaking rather than being defined by her connection to literary giant Hermann Hesse (he was her father-in-law), a fate that befell many women artists of her generation. The screenings offered only a glimpse of a wider body of work currently being restored by the Cinémathèque Suisse which hopefully will reach audiences soon.
Asphalt Guerrilla (Guerrilha no Asfalto), by the Portuguese director Edgar Pêra, also belongs on this poetic list, included in the “Out of Competition” section. Pêra’s poetics deliver a genuine punk punch, a multilayered mockumentary purposedly blurring the lines between (auto)fiction, documentary, and film essay.
Framed as a restoration of an old project focused on Portuguese urban guerrillas in the aftermath of the Carnation Revolution (1974) that brought down 50 years of a fascist regime, Pêra confounds the register of political guerrilla with guerrilla filmmaking, evolving into a reflection on the development of film-making in the last 50 years up to a critical, scary use of artificial intelligence.
Made in Switzerland
Basil da Cunha’s O Jacaré (Crocodile), the final chapter of his “Reboleira Trilogy”, is the Swiss film representative in the main competition. Da Cunha’s art and life blend closely in the trilogy, that started with O Fim do Mundo (The End of the World, 2019), followed by Manga d’Terra (2023).
Son of Portuguese immigrants in Switzerland, da Cunha studied film before moving to Portugal. Arriving there penniless, he ended up in the Reboleira district, a shanty town north of Lisbon, mostly inhabited by Cape-Verdean immigrants and their offspring. He soon began making films with residents, drawing on the experiences of friends and neighbours.
Over almost 20 years, a genuine community of collaborators has gathered around da Cunha, even though the Reboleira of the first films doesn’t exist anymore, swallowed by urban expansion and real estate speculation beyond the Portuguese capital, with the inevitable evictions and dispersion.
In Cineasti del Presente, Mateo Ybarra’s Small Talk is a story set in Switzerland’s last finishing school and will certainly attract a wide audience fascinated by the universe of luxury and its codes.
None of them won a prize this year – in fact, the last Swiss film to take a major prize in Locarno was Milagros Mumenthaler’s Abrir puertas y ventanas (2011); before her, you have to go back to 1985, with Fredi Murer’s Alpine Fire.
But it was a Swiss film, Petra Volpe’s first English-speaking movie Frank & Louis, that won this year’s Prix du Public, the prize awarded to the most popular film shown in Locarno’s open-air Piazza Grande screen, voted by the audience. A perfect example of direct democracy in action.
